The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Experts asked to predict political events often perform little better than chance, and those with the most confident, unified worldviews tend to perform worst. Forecasters who draw on many perspectives, adjust their views readily and express predictions as probabilities do better. The difference lies less in what forecasters know than in how they hold what they know.
questions.solution: Option 1 captures the contrast between how knowledge is held and how much there is. Option 3 overstates; some forecasters do better. Option 2 is unsupported. Option 4 is an unsupported prescription.
options: Forecasting accuracy depends more on flexible, probabilistic habits of thought than on the amount of knowledge a forecaster possesses.
Experts know less than non-experts about politics.
Political events are inherently unpredictable.
Confident forecasters should be ignored entirely.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Antibiotics added to animal feed in small doses make livestock grow faster, which is why the practice spread. But every dose gives bacteria an opportunity to evolve resistance, and resistant bacteria do not stay on farms. The farmer gains the benefit of faster growth, while the cost of lost effectiveness is shared by everyone who may one day need an antibiotic that no longer works.
questions.solution: Option 4 captures the private-benefit, shared-cost structure. Option 3 contradicts "do not stay on farms", and option 1 contradicts the first sentence. Option 2 is unsupported.
options: Antibiotics do not make livestock grow faster.
Antibiotics in feed should be used only in larger doses.
Resistant bacteria remain confined to farms.
Routine antibiotic use in livestock yields private gains for farmers while spreading the cost of resistance across society.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Ancient city walls were built for defence, but their most lasting effect was often economic. Gates were points at which goods could be counted and taxed, and markets clustered around them. ____ Long after the walls ceased to matter militarily, the street patterns they had created continued to shape where commerce happened.
questions.solution: The blank should generalise the economic role before "Long after ... continued to shape" commerce. Option 2 does. Option 3 could fit only loosely and does not bridge to the continuing effect. Options 4 and 1 are tangential.
options: Some cities had more than one ring of walls.
The walls thus organised the city's trade as much as they protected its inhabitants.
Many walls were demolished in the nineteenth century to make way for roads.
Siege warfare changed dramatically with the introduction of artillery.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Volunteers who count birds in their gardens every winter have produced one of the largest datasets in ecology. The counts are imperfect: volunteers differ in skill and attention, and gardens are not a random sample of the landscape. ____ What is lost in precision for any one count is regained in the scale and duration of the whole.
questions.solution: The final sentence weighs precision against scale, so the blank must introduce scale as a compensation. Option 2 does. Option 1 stays with the imperfection. Options 3 and 4 are irrelevant.
options: Professional ecologists are generally more accurate than volunteers.
But the sheer number of participants and the decades over which they have counted allow many such errors to average out.
Birds visit gardens more often in winter than in summer.
Some volunteers also count butterflies in summer.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Economists sometimes treat preferences as fixed, so that policies can be judged by how well they satisfy what people already want. ____ A policy that makes cycling safe may produce cyclists who now prefer cycling, and judging it by the preferences that existed before it was introduced misses what it has done.
questions.solution: The example shows a policy creating a preference, so the blank must state that policies change preferences. Option 1 does. Option 3 is a different objection. Options 2 and 4 are irrelevant.
options: Yet many policies change preferences as well as satisfying them.
Cycling is cheaper than driving in most cities.
Preferences are difficult to measure precisely.
Some economists have studied transport policy in detail.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Handwritten letters from past centuries are prized by historians for their candour. Writers who expected only one reader said things they would never have published. ____ A letter that seems spontaneous may have been drafted with an eye to the collection in which it now sits.
questions.solution: The last sentence warns that letters may have been written for posterity, so the blank must introduce that awareness. Option 2 does. The others are tangential.
options: Postal services became cheaper during the nineteenth century.
Yet some letter-writers, especially the famous, wrote knowing that their correspondence would be kept and eventually read by others.
Historians also use diaries as sources.
Many letters were lost in fires or floods.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

A medicine that relieves symptoms quickly may sell better than one that cures more slowly, even if the second is better for the patient. Patients judge treatments by how they feel in the following days, and physicians, under pressure to satisfy them, may prescribe accordingly. ____ The market for treatments thus rewards what is perceptible rather than what is effective, unless something intervenes to make the slower benefits visible.
questions.solution: The conclusion contrasts the perceptible with the effective, so the blank must explain why slow benefits go unrewarded. Option 2 does. Option 3 is plausible background but does not explain the asymmetry. Options 4 and 1 are irrelevant.
options: Many patients prefer tablets to injections.
Long-term outcomes, by contrast, are noticed late and are rarely traced back to the treatment that produced them.
Pharmaceutical companies spend heavily on marketing.
Physicians are generally well informed about new treatments.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Instruction manuals are often blamed when people misuse a device. ____ A design that requires a manual to prevent dangerous errors has, in a sense, already failed, since most users will never read it.
questions.solution: The next sentence shifts blame to design, so the blank must make that shift. Option 1 does. The others do not lead to it.
options: But the deeper fault frequently lies in a design that invites the error in the first place.
Some devices come with manuals in several languages.
People who read manuals tend to be more careful in general.
Manuals are now usually provided online rather than in print.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. Before the printing press, a book's text could change every time it was copied.
  2. Scribes corrected what they took to be errors and sometimes introduced new ones.
  3. Printing fixed a text in hundreds of identical copies, making it possible to cite a page with confidence.
  4. Paper was cheaper than parchment, which reduced the cost of making books.
  5. Scholarly argument came to depend on the assumption that everyone was reading the same words.
questions.solution: 1-2-3-5 concerns textual stability and its effect on scholarship. Sentence 4, about the cost of materials, is a related fact about book production but does not belong to the argument about fixed texts.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. A city's trees cool the streets beneath them by several degrees on hot days.
  2. The benefit is unevenly distributed, because poorer neighbourhoods tend to have fewer trees.
  3. Residents of those neighbourhoods therefore bear more of the burden of extreme heat.
  4. Planting programmes that target the least shaded districts can narrow this gap.
  5. Some species of tree release pollen that aggravates allergies.
questions.solution: 1-2-3-4 runs from benefit to inequality to remedy. Sentence 5 introduces a cost of trees unconnected to the distributional argument.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. Chess engines now play far better than any human.
  2. Yet chess remains popular, and top human players attract large audiences.
  3. Spectators are interested in human struggle, error and recovery, not merely in perfect moves.
  4. Engines have also changed how professionals prepare, since every opening can now be tested by machine.
  5. A contest between machines, however brilliant, offers little of this drama.
questions.solution: 1-2-3-5 explains why human chess survives machine superiority. Sentence 4 concerns how engines changed preparation, which is on-topic but not about why spectators still watch humans.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. Minimum wage laws are often debated as if their only effect were on employment.
  2. Employers facing higher wage costs may respond in other ways: by cutting hours, reducing training or raising prices.
  3. Which response predominates depends on the industry and the local labour market.
  4. A study that measures only job numbers may therefore miss most of what the law changed.
  5. In some countries minimum wages are set by government; in others they are negotiated between unions and employers.
questions.solution: 1-2-3-4 argues that effects extend beyond employment counts. Sentence 5 is about how minimum wages are set, which does not contribute to that argument.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. The habit of taking notes by hand is sometimes defended as better for learning than typing.
  2. Writing by hand is slower, which forces the student to summarise rather than transcribe.
  3. Summarising requires processing the material, which aids later recall.
  4. Some students find handwritten notes harder to search and reorganise afterwards.
  5. Typing, by allowing near-verbatim transcription, can let the material pass through without being understood.
questions.solution: 1-2-3-5 is a causal argument about note-taking and learning. Sentence 4 raises a practical drawback of handwritten notes, not part of the causal argument about processing and learning.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. A river that floods regularly deposits fertile silt on the surrounding plain.
  2. Embankments built to prevent flooding also prevent this deposit.
  3. Farmland protected from floods may therefore slowly lose its fertility.
  4. Meanwhile, silt that would have spread across the plain accumulates in the riverbed, raising it and making catastrophic breaches more likely.
  5. Some of the world's oldest civilisations arose on river plains.
questions.solution: 1-2-3-4 analyses the unintended consequences of embankments. Sentence 5 is a general historical remark, tempting because of its topic, but outside the causal chain.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. Open-source software is written by volunteers and companies who give it away.
  2. Much of the world's commercial infrastructure now depends on it.
  3. Some critical components are maintained by a handful of unpaid people.
  4. When such a component fails, the damage can spread to thousands of firms that never contributed to it.
  5. Software licences can be difficult for non-lawyers to understand.
questions.solution: 1-2-3-4 traces dependence on under-maintained open-source components. Sentence 5 on licences is a different issue.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. A word's etymology is often cited as evidence of its "true" meaning.
  2. But meanings drift, and a word's origin may tell us little about how it is used now.
  3. Many English words of Latin origin entered the language through French.
  4. To insist on the original sense is to confuse the history of a word with its present function.
  5. Such insistence is usually a rhetorical move rather than a linguistic argument.
questions.solution: 1-2-4-5 argues against the etymological fallacy. Sentence 3 is an etymological fact that does not contribute to the argument, though its subject makes it tempting.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. They were, in effect, being paid to create the problem they were paid to solve.
  2. A colonial administration once offered a reward for every dead cobra brought to its offices.
  3. Residents soon began breeding cobras in order to collect the reward.
  4. Worse still, when the scheme was cancelled, the breeders released their now-worthless snakes.
questions.solution: 2 sets up the reward; 3 gives the response; 1 ("They ... in effect") interprets it; 4 ("Worse still") gives the ending, which needs a prior negative judgement. 4 could not precede 1, since 1 comments on the breeding, not the release.

questions.question:
The five sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the five numbers (e.g. 21435).

  1. Such plans assumed that the future could be read from the trend of the recent past.
  2. In the decades after the war, many cities drew up master plans projecting traffic growth for thirty years ahead.
  3. Acting on that assumption, authorities widened roads and drove highways through neighbourhoods to meet the projected demand.
  4. The new capacity was soon filled, and the projections appeared to have been vindicated.
  5. In fact the projections had helped to produce the traffic they predicted.
questions.solution: 2 introduces the plans; 1 ("Such plans") states their assumption; 3 ("Acting on that assumption") describes their implementation; 4 gives the apparent vindication; 5 ("In fact") reverses it. 3 cannot precede 1, because "Such plans" must follow 2 directly.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. As a result, the same disease could be described in incompatible ways by different hospitals.
  2. Before international classifications existed, each country recorded causes of death in its own terms.
  3. Comparing mortality across hospitals, let alone across borders, was therefore nearly impossible.
  4. Often, even within a country, practices varied from one institution to another.
questions.solution: 2 introduces national terms; 4 ("even within a country") extends the variation to institutions; 1 ("As a result ... different hospitals") follows from 4; 3 ("across hospitals, let alone across borders") concludes and must follow 1.

questions.question:
The five sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the five numbers (e.g. 21435).

  1. The answer, surprisingly, was that the most productive lands were often the most heavily taxed into poverty.
  2. A historian studying old revenue records asked why certain fertile districts had remained poor for centuries.
  3. Assessments had been fixed when yields were highest and were never revised downward.
  4. When soils became exhausted, peasants owed the same tax on smaller harvests.
  5. Fertility, in other words, had become a liability inscribed in the ledger.
questions.solution: 2 poses the question; 1 ("The answer") answers it; 3 explains the mechanism; 4 continues it ("the same tax"); 5 ("in other words") sums up.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. Yet the mutineers, in the logbook, appear only as a list of names and punishments.
  2. The captain's logbook records weather, positions and provisions in meticulous detail.
  3. Their reasons, the conditions they endured and the arguments among them went unrecorded.
  4. Historians must reconstruct the mutiny from what such silence implies.
questions.solution: 2 introduces the log's detail; 1 ("Yet") contrasts it with the treatment of the mutineers; 3 ("Their") elaborates the omission; 4 ("such silence") concludes.

questions.question:
The five sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the five numbers (e.g. 21435).

  1. This lowered costs but also made every buyer dependent on a single supplier's continued willingness to sell.
  2. For centuries, villages produced most of their own tools, cloth and food.
  3. Industrial production replaced many of these local crafts with cheaper goods from distant factories.
  4. When trade was interrupted by war, the absence of local skills turned a disruption into a crisis.
  5. Efficiency in normal times had been purchased with fragility in abnormal ones.
questions.solution: 2 sets the baseline; 3 describes the replacement; 1 ("This") gives its double effect; 4 tests it under disruption; 5 draws the lesson.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. The figure is cited so often that few think to check it.
  2. A widely quoted statistic claims that people use only a tenth of their brains.
  3. Those who do check find that brain imaging shows virtually all regions are active over the course of a day.
  4. Its persistence owes more to its appeal than to any evidence.
questions.solution: 2 introduces the claim; 1 ("The figure ... few think to check") sets up 3 ("Those who do check"), which refutes it with evidence; 4 ("Its persistence") explains its survival despite that. 4 before 3 would explain persistence before showing it is false.

questions.question:
The five sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the five numbers (e.g. 21435).

  1. Each new layer was added to solve a problem created by the previous one.
  2. The tax code of many countries has grown to thousands of pages.
  3. Exemptions, for instance, created loopholes, which required rules to close them, which created further exemptions.
  4. No one designed this complexity; it accumulated.
  5. Simplification is therefore harder than it looks, since every rule is someone's protection.
questions.solution: 2 states the size; 1 explains the layering; 3 ("for instance") illustrates the layering; 4 ("this complexity") sums up the process; 5 ("therefore") draws the implication.

questions.question: The central concern of the passage is that:
questions.solution: The passage moves from problems of testimony to the "prior question" of why documents exist, arguing that the archive's composition distorts conclusions even under careful reading (para 3). Option 4 concerns testimony, which the author says is already handled. Option 3 overstates; alternative sources "have their own biases". Option 1 is exactly the false inference the author warns against.
options: marginal groups were more often involved in legal disputes than other groups
the selective way archives were created can distort historical conclusions even when individual documents are read critically
historians should abandon official records in favour of oral and archaeological sources
historical documents frequently contain deliberate falsehoods that historians fail to detect

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as an example of the "distortion" discussed in the third paragraph?
questions.solution: The distortion arises from the composition of the collection: a group appearing "mainly through court cases will seem more ... disorderly". Option 3 matches this. Options 4, 2 and 1 are problems of testimony or accuracy within documents, which the first paragraph distinguishes from the archive's composition.
options: A historian finds that a memoir and a set of letters give conflicting accounts of a meeting.
A historian discovers that a chronicle misdates a battle by several years.
A historian concludes that a fishing village was unusually violent because almost every surviving mention of it comes from criminal court proceedings.
A historian concludes that a guild's records exaggerate its members' wealth because the guild wished to impress the authorities.

questions.question: The comparison with an ecologist estimating a population is used to illustrate:
questions.solution: The ecologist analogy follows "estimating what the archive omits from what it includes", that is, inferring the unobserved from the observed sample. Option 3 introduces a ranking the author never makes. Option 1 concerns the other response. Option 2 is explained earlier and is not the point of the analogy.
options: the difficulty of dating oral traditions and archaeological finds
the reason that marginal groups were rarely recorded by institutions
the superiority of scientific methods over traditional historical ones
an approach that infers the scale of what is missing from the pattern of what has been preserved

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the two responses described in the fourth paragraph is best described as:
questions.solution: The author notes both "accept that silence is itself a kind of evidence" (appreciation), but also their biases and that "neither can recover what was never written down" (qualification). Option 3 contradicts that clause. Option 2 is harsher than the text, and option 1 ignores the evaluation.
options: neutral, since the author does not evaluate them
dismissive, because both introduce worse biases than official archives
enthusiastic, because together they solve the problem of the archive's silences
qualified appreciation, recognising their value while noting that neither can fully overcome the archive's limitations

questions.question: According to the passage, removing a height limit in a neighbourhood may produce little new construction because:
questions.solution: Para 2: where "prices sit just below such a threshold ... additional floors would cost more than they could be sold for". Options 1, 2 and 3 are not given as reasons in the passage.
options: developers prefer to build in the suburbs
residents of such neighbourhoods oppose new buildings
the approval process remains lengthy even after the limit is removed
prices there may be too low to cover the higher per-square-metre cost of building beyond a certain height

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that critics who cite luxury towers as evidence against deregulation:
questions.solution: Para 3: such critics "are mistaken about the long-run effects, but they are describing accurately what deregulation first produces". Option 1 contradicts that. Option 3 is not attributed to them. Option 2 misuses the mid-rise example.
options: are right that deregulation never benefits those on lower incomes
have been proved wrong by the expansion of mid-rise housing
misunderstand the costs of building tall structures
correctly observe deregulation's initial effects but draw the wrong conclusion about its eventual consequences

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's explanation of the "low buildings punctuated by isolated towers" pattern?
questions.solution: The author attributes the missing middle to mid-rise construction being costly relative to its value, citing code changes that cut its cost. Option 3 shows that lowering exactly that cost raised mid-rise building alone, which strengthens the mechanism. Option 4 offers a rival, demand-side explanation. Option 1 is irrelevant to cost thresholds. Option 2 points back to regulation.
options: Towers in such cities are mostly occupied by offices rather than housing.
Height limits in such cities are set separately for each neighbourhood.
After a country permitted single-staircase designs for six-to-eight-storey buildings, applications for buildings of that height rose sharply while applications for towers were unchanged.
In a city with such a pattern, survey data show that most residents prefer to live in detached houses.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author's overall position?
questions.solution: The author accepts the regulatory evidence (para 1) and the final paragraph calls regulation "one constraint among several". Option 2 contradicts that. Option 4 is denied: "None of this is an argument for keeping restrictive rules". Option 1 overstates; mid-rise is called costly.
options: Mid-rise housing is always the most efficient form of urban development.
Building regulations are the only significant obstacle to housing supply.
Regulation does restrict housing supply, but the cost structure of construction shapes where and how supply responds once rules are relaxed.
Deregulation benefits only the wealthy and should be resisted.

questions.question: The passage is primarily concerned with:
questions.solution: The extreme cases are set aside in para 2, and the rest of the passage tests tact against the strict view and alternatives. Option 4 is not the author's stance; para 3 challenges the strict view's defence. Option 1 is a side example. Option 3 contradicts "conventions are not always shared".
options: arguing that lying to a murderer is morally required
examining whether everyday tact can be reconciled with views about the wrongness of lying
showing that politeness conventions are universally shared
defending the strict view that lying is always wrong

questions.question: The author's objection to the defence that tact is permissible because it avoids literal falsehood rests on the claim that:
questions.solution: Para 3: "a carefully chosen truth that is designed to produce a false belief manipulates no less than a lie does." Options 3 and 1 are unsupported. Option 2 overstates; the author presents a dilemma rather than declaring the view baseless.
options: tactful speakers always intend to cause harm
the strict view has no principled basis
literal truth is impossible to achieve in ordinary conversation
if deception is wrong because it manipulates beliefs, then a truth selected to produce a false belief is open to the same objection

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the "third possibility" described in the fourth paragraph?
questions.solution: The third possibility holds that tact does not deceive because listeners understand the convention and form no false belief. Option 2 shows that listeners did form false beliefs, which undercuts the view's core claim. Option 4 bears on whether conventions are shared, but differences between cultures need not affect exchanges within one culture, so it is weaker. Options 1 and 3 do not address whether tact deceives.
options: Most people say they prefer honest friends to tactful ones.
In a study, people who received polite praise for their work frequently believed the work had been genuinely well received and were surprised by later criticism.
Tactful answers are more common among close friends than among strangers.
Polite conventions differ between cultures.

questions.question: The examples of the dinner, the presentation and the photograph in the second paragraph serve to:
questions.solution: They introduce "the territory of tact", far from the extreme cases on which the debate "is usually conducted". Option 1 contradicts "few people tell a flat lie". Option 3 overstates; the author poses a dilemma. Option 2 introduces cultures, which these examples do not involve.
options: show that people frequently tell flat lies to spare others' feelings
illustrate the conventions of polite conversation in different cultures
prove that the strict view is mistaken
establish a common class of situations that the debate over extreme cases tends to overlook

questions.question: According to the passage, why do many credit schemes rely on models rather than direct measurement?
questions.solution: Para 2 explains that detecting the change "requires many samples ... Such sampling is expensive, and many credit schemes rely instead on models". The other options are not stated.
options: Farmers refuse to allow sampling on their land.
Models are required by law.
Detecting small changes against large natural variation requires extensive and costly sampling.
Soil samples cannot be taken below the surface.

questions.question: The finding about reduced tillage described in the third paragraph implies that:
questions.solution: Gains near the surface were "offset by losses lower down"; stopping ploughing concentrated carbon "without necessarily increasing the total". Option 4 overstates ("always lowers"). Option 3 is not claimed. Option 1 contradicts "losses lower down".
options: deeper soil layers contain no carbon
a measured increase in surface carbon need not mean that the soil as a whole holds more carbon
ploughing increases the total carbon stored in soil
reduced tillage always lowers the total carbon in soil

questions.question: The author's contrast between avoided fuel emissions and stored soil carbon in the fourth paragraph assumes that:
questions.solution: The contrast relies on the offset emission continuing "to warm the planet" over a century while soil carbon may be lost meanwhile. Option 3 states that assumption. Option 4 reverses the passage ("speeds"). Options 2 and 1 are not relied upon.
options: farmers are generally dishonest about their practices
soil carbon credits are cheaper than other offsets
the warming effect of an emission that a credit offsets continues over a period long enough for stored soil carbon to be released
warmer climates slow the decomposition of organic matter

questions.question: Which of the following best summarises the author's conclusion?
questions.solution: The final paragraph defends the practices but warns against treating stored carbon "as equivalent to a tonne of emissions avoided". Option 2 contradicts that, option 3 is stronger than the author, and option 4 is never claimed.
options: Soil carbon practices have real benefits, but their carbon gains are too uncertain to be treated as equivalent to avoided emissions.
Practices that increase soil carbon should be abandoned.
Soil carbon credits are fraudulent and should be banned.
Better models will soon make soil carbon credits fully reliable.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

When a word acquires a new meaning, dictionaries record the change only after it has spread, and usage guides condemn it for a generation before conceding defeat. The lag is often treated as a failure of the guardians of language, who are accused of resisting the inevitable. But the lag performs a function. A meaning that survives a generation of disapproval has shown that it fills a need the old vocabulary did not; one that fades was perhaps a fashion. Resistance, in other words, is the test through which new usage earns its place.
questions.solution: The paragraph reframes the lag as functional: survival through disapproval shows a real need. Option 2 captures this. Option 4 adopts the criticism the passage rejects. Option 3 ignores the meanings that fade. Option 1 is unsupported as a generalisation.
options: New meanings usually fade within a generation.
Resistance to new meanings, though often derided, acts as a filter that separates lasting changes from passing fashions.
Usage guides are always eventually proved wrong about new meanings.
Dictionaries are too slow to record new meanings and should be updated more often.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Forecasts of technological change are usually wrong in a characteristic way. In the short term they overestimate how quickly a new technology will be adopted, because they assume that a working prototype is close to a working product and ignore the slow work of building supply chains, training users and rewriting rules. Over the long term they underestimate its effects, because they imagine the technology slotting into existing practices rather than reshaping them. The same forecaster can therefore be disappointed in year five and astonished in year twenty.
questions.solution: Option 1 captures the two-directional error and its two causes. Option 4 misses the long-term underestimate. Option 2 turns an illustration into a rule. Option 3 confuses delay with failure.
options: Technological forecasts tend to err in opposite directions over different horizons: too fast on adoption, too narrow on eventual impact.
New technologies take about twenty years to be adopted.
Prototypes are rarely close to finished products, which is why technologies fail.
Forecasters are consistently too optimistic about new technologies.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Biographers of scientists are drawn to the moment of discovery: the sudden insight, the decisive experiment. The archive rarely supports such scenes. Notebooks show ideas returned to over years, abandoned and revived, often half-formulated long before their author recognised what they meant. ____ The drama that readers expect is therefore usually supplied in retrospect, by the scientist's later memory or the biographer's art.
questions.solution: The blank must link the notebooks' gradualness to "drama ... supplied in retrospect". Option 3 does so by recasting the moment as gradual. Option 1 is background. Option 4 supports sudden discovery and cuts against the paragraph. Option 2 contradicts the reliance on archives.
options: Most scientists keep careful notebooks throughout their careers.
Biographers rarely consult the archives of the scientists they write about.
What looks in hindsight like a single moment was typically a gradual recognition with no clear point of arrival.
Some discoveries are made by accident in the laboratory.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Small shops in old market streets often survive competition from supermarkets not by matching their prices but by offering what a large store cannot: credit to known customers, goods in tiny quantities and advice from someone who knows the household. ____ When such shops close, the loss is felt most by those who depended on these services rather than by the average shopper.
questions.solution: The last sentence speaks of those who "depended on these services", so the blank should identify who that is. Option 1 does. Option 3 restates background. Options 2 and 4 do not bridge to the final sentence.
options: These advantages matter most to customers with irregular incomes or limited storage space.
Many market streets have recently been pedestrianised.
Supermarkets usually offer lower prices because they buy in bulk.
Shopkeepers in such streets often belong to the same families for generations.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. A rumour spreads not because people believe it but because it is useful to pass on.
  2. Sharing it signals that one is well informed and offers the listener a token of trust.
  3. Its accuracy is therefore a secondary matter for those who repeat it.
  4. Corrections, which offer no such social reward, travel more slowly and reach fewer people.
  5. Studies have found that false news stories online are more often novel than true ones.
questions.solution: 1-2-3-4 develops a social-function account: rumours are passed on for what sharing signals, and corrections lack that reward. Sentence 5 introduces novelty as an explanation, which is related to the topic of false stories but does not belong to this social-reward argument.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. Nineteenth-century galleries hung paintings frame to frame, from floor to ceiling.
  2. Visitors faced with hundreds of works gave each only a few seconds.
  3. Curators gradually reduced the number of works on show, leaving bare wall around each.
  4. The storerooms of large museums hold far more objects than are ever displayed.
  5. The empty wall became, in effect, an instruction to look for longer.
questions.solution: 1 → 2 → 3 → 5 traces how sparse hanging was meant to lengthen attention. Sentence 4, on museum storage, is on-topic and might seem to follow 3, but it shifts from viewers' attention to collection size and plays no part in the argument.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. That expectation, however, assumed that the cost of keeping a record would remain the main constraint on memory.
  2. Early theorists of the information age predicted that cheap storage would make societies better at remembering.
  3. Once storage became almost free, the constraint shifted from keeping to finding.
  4. The result is an abundance of preserved material that is, in practice, as inaccessible as if it had been discarded.
questions.solution: 2 states the prediction; 1 ("That expectation") identifies its hidden premise; 3 shows the premise failing ("the constraint shifted"); 4 ("The result") states the consequence. 3 cannot precede 1, because "the constraint" needs 1 to introduce it.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. This made the gardens a record of the empire's commercial ambitions as much as a scientific collection.
  2. Botanical gardens in the colonial era were rarely founded only for the study of plants.
  3. Many were charged with acclimatising crops that could be grown profitably in other territories.
  4. That record has outlasted the empires themselves: some of today's plantation economies trace their origins to seedlings raised in such gardens.
questions.solution: 2 opens; 3 ("Many were charged") specifies the non-scientific role; 1 ("This") interprets it; 4 ("That record") must follow 1, which introduces the gardens as a record; so 2341 is ruled out.

questions.question: The main argument of the passage is that:
questions.solution: The passage traces the cross-subsidy (para 1), its loss (para 2), the case of local reporting (para 3) and the resulting scarcity "whose value lay in its use by the few" (para 5). Option 4 is a view the author sets aside as too easy. Option 2 overstates; subscriptions fail for most local outlets. Option 1 is unsupported.
options: advertisers are responsible for the decline of foreign reporting
subscriptions are the best solution to the problems of local journalism
the unbundling of news has removed a hidden cross-subsidy, leaving reporting valuable to small, concerned audiences without a means of support
digital media have made all news coverage more trivial

questions.question: The author's statement that metrics "are silent on why it mattered" implies that:
questions.solution: The sentence follows the point that a few hundred affected readers may make a report valuable "measured by its consequences". Option 1 contradicts "The metrics are not wrong about how many people read". Options 3 and 4 are unsupported.
options: click counts are frequently inaccurate
the value of some reporting lies in its effects through a small readership rather than in the size of that readership
local readers do not use the internet
editors should ignore audience data entirely

questions.question: Which of the following situations most closely parallels the "mechanism" whose loss is described in the final paragraph?
questions.solution: The mechanism is a bundle in which many pay unknowingly for material used by few. A library fee that funds rarely used reference works matches it. Options 2 and 4 are unbundled, item-by-item payments. Option 3 is about advertising support, not cross-subsidy.
options: A single membership fee at a public library pays for the whole collection, including specialised reference works that few members ever consult.
A streaming service charges extra for each film watched.
A software firm offers a free version supported by advertising.
A charity asks donors to fund a specific project of their choosing.

questions.question: According to the passage, subscriptions are a difficult model for most local outlets because:
questions.solution: Para 4: a town "may contain enough readers to support a newspaper through advertising but not enough willing subscribers ... especially when much of what the paper reports can be found ... for free". Option 1 overstates ("any news"). Options 4 and 3 are not stated.
options: local readers are unwilling to pay for any news
a small population may not provide enough paying subscribers, particularly when summaries are available for free
national titles prevent local outlets from offering subscriptions
advertisers refuse to support subscription papers

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
questions.solution: The passage argues for a two-way view and ends with "a partnership whose terms neither party chose". Option 2 is the view qualified at the outset. Option 1 is explicitly rejected ("should not be taken literally"). Option 4 contradicts the skeletal evidence.
options: Wheat, in a literal sense, domesticated human beings.
Domestication was a deliberate human project that succeeded completely.
Domestication was a reciprocal process in which humans were reshaped by the species they cultivated, largely without intending the outcome.
Early farmers were healthier than foragers.

questions.question: The author's comment that "the trap, if it was one, was built from the accumulated consequences of reasonable choices" suggests that:
questions.solution: The sentence follows the list of consequences (growing populations, cleared land, lost knowledge) that made abandonment hard. Option 2 captures this. Option 3 contradicts "reasonable choices". Options 1 and 4 are unsupported.
options: foraging was always more productive than farming
the difficulty of returning to foraging arose from cumulative effects rather than from any single mistaken decision
early farmers were foolish to adopt agriculture
agriculture was imposed on early communities by outsiders

questions.question: The discussion of dogs in the fourth paragraph serves primarily to:
questions.solution: It opens "The two-way view also changes how we think about animals" and describes selection in both directions. Options 4 and 3 make claims about chronology and importance that the passage does not make. Option 1 contradicts the account of less fearful wolves.
options: explain why wolves avoid human settlements
extend the reciprocal account of domestication from crops to animals
argue that dogs were more important than wheat to early humans
show that animals were domesticated before plants

questions.question: The author's use of skeletal evidence in the second paragraph to suggest that domestication was not "obviously advantageous" to early farmers assumes that:
questions.solution: Drawing a conclusion about farming from skeletal comparisons requires that the differences be due to farming and not to unrepresentative samples. Option 2 states that. Option 3 is an extreme the argument does not need. Option 1 is narrower than what is required, and option 4 is irrelevant.
options: shorter stature is always caused by heavier labour
the skeletal differences reflect the farmers' way of life rather than differences in the populations that happened to be sampled
foragers never suffered from poor health
early farmers kept careful records of their health

questions.question: The author's main purpose is to:
questions.solution: The last paragraph distinguishes explanation that replaces experience (rightly resisted) from explanation that directs attention and transmits skill (useful). Option 3 is contradicted by paras 3–4. Option 2 is denied in para 1. Option 1 contradicts para 2.
options: prove that scores fully determine musical experience
show that performers are generally anti-intellectual
argue that musical analysis should be abandoned
clarify the conditions under which explanation of music is valuable and those under which musicians rightly resist it

questions.question: According to the passage, why is analysis less successful at accounting for a phrase held "a fraction longer than expected"?
questions.solution: Para 2: the effect depends on expectation, timing and attention, and "the score does not contain it". Option 2 overstates; para 2 says analysis favours recurring features but does not claim such moments never recur. Options 4 and 3 are unsupported.
options: The effect depends on features of performance and listening that the score does not record.
Such moments never recur in other pieces.
Listeners cannot perceive differences in timing.
Analysts dislike discussing individual performances.

questions.question: The example of a theme returning "after a long departure" is used to show that:
questions.solution: The example supports the claim that analysis "does not explain the emotion so much as prepare the ground for it". Option 2 overstates what the author says analysis does. Options 3 and 4 are unsupported.
options: structural understanding can enrich emotional response rather than replace it
analysis fully explains why music moves listeners
repetition is the most important feature of musical form
untrained listeners enjoy music more than trained ones

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that a teacher's explanation that "stops at a point where the teacher says that it simply sounds better":
questions.solution: Para 4: "a partial explanation that guides practice is not worthless merely because it does not reach all the way down", and reasoning lets the student apply it to other music. Option 2 is denied. Options 1 and 3 run against the paragraph's preference for explanation.
options: shows that the teacher does not understand the music
is worthless because it is incomplete
should be replaced by demonstration alone
can still be valuable if it helps the student apply the reasoning elsewhere

questions.question: According to the passage, governments rely on numbers mainly because:
questions.solution: Para 1 offers the explanation that numbers are used "where trust in judgement is weak"; para 2 calls the number "less accurate but more defensible". Option 4 contradicts that. Options 2 and 3 are not the author's explanation.
options: quantification offers a defensible basis for decisions where trust in personal judgement is weak
officials lack the experience to make decisions
the public prefers numbers to words
numbers are always more accurate than human judgement

questions.question: The author's claim that quantification "can thus be read as a sign of weakness rather than strength" implies that:
questions.solution: The claim follows the observation that contested professions "adopted numbers more readily", so adopting them signals contested standing. Option 1 confuses weak authority with incompetence. Options 2 and 3 overstate.
options: professions that adopt numbers are incompetent
medicine has never used numbers
strong professions always produce better outcomes
the adoption of measurement may indicate that a profession's personal authority is contested

questions.question: Which of the following best exemplifies the problem described in the fourth paragraph?
questions.solution: The fourth paragraph describes people improving the number "at the expense of what it was meant to indicate". Option 4 is a direct example of that. Option 3 is just a statistic. Options 1 and 2 do not involve gaming a measure.
options: A government replaces a committee with an independent auditor.
A school is praised for its examination results by parents.
A city publishes crime statistics that show a decline in burglary.
Police officers, assessed by the number of cases closed, begin recording minor incidents as resolved without investigating them.

questions.question: The final paragraph serves primarily to:
questions.solution: It opens "it would be wrong to wish simply for a return to discretion", notes that numbers opened decisions to scrutiny, and ends with the warning about defensible versus correct decisions. Options 3 and 2 contradict it. Option 1 is not discussed there.
options: summarise the history of measurement in medicine
argue for a return to discretionary decision-making
reject quantification as harmful
balance the preceding criticism by noting the benefits of numbers and warning against confusing defensibility with correctness

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Collectors often justify their acquisitions as acts of preservation: an object bought is an object saved from neglect. Yet the market that collectors create also gives value to objects that were never in danger, and the prospect of a sale can encourage their removal from the places where they had survived for centuries. Preservation by purchase may thus increase the very risk it claims to reduce.
questions.solution: Option 4 captures both the justification and the self-defeating effect. Option 3 imputes motives the passage does not discuss. Option 2 is a broader claim than the passage makes. Option 1 contradicts "never in danger".
options: Most collected objects were in danger of being neglected.
Objects are safest when left in their original locations.
Collectors are mainly motivated by profit rather than preservation.
Collecting, justified as preservation, can create a market that encourages the removal and endangerment of objects.

questions.question:
The passage given below is followed by four summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Diet studies frequently report that people who eat a particular food live longer. Such findings are hard to interpret, because people who choose that food tend to differ in other ways: they may be wealthier, exercise more or smoke less. Statistical adjustments can account for differences that were measured, but not for those that were not. The healthiest-looking foods may therefore owe part of their reputation to the habits of those who eat them.
questions.solution: Option 4 states the confounding problem. Option 1 asserts a causal claim the passage questions. Option 3 contradicts "but not for those that were not". Option 2 is an unsupported prescription.
options: Wealthy people live longer because they eat healthier food.
People should not change their diets on the basis of research.
Statistical adjustment removes all bias from diet studies.
Observational links between foods and longevity may reflect the other characteristics of those who eat them.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

A cartographer drawing a coastline must decide how much detail to include. A map at a large scale can show every inlet; at a small scale, the same coast becomes a smooth curve. ____ Mapmakers have therefore learned to state the scale at which a length was measured, since without it the figure has no fixed meaning.
questions.solution: The final sentence's "the scale at which a length was measured" requires a prior sentence linking length to the level of detail. Option 2 provides this. The other options do not lead to that conclusion.
options: Small-scale maps are more useful for navigation.
The measured length of the coast depends on that choice, growing as finer features are included.
Modern satellites have made coastal maps more accurate.
Coastlines change over time because of erosion.

questions.question:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Read the paragraph and choose the option that best completes it.

Hospitals that publish their surgeons' success rates hope to inform patients and motivate improvement. ____ A surgeon who declines a risky operation improves her figures while a patient who needed the operation goes without it. Publication, intended to raise standards, can thus reward caution at the patient's expense.
questions.solution: The next sentence describes risk-avoidance, so the blank must introduce that incentive. Option 4 does. Options 2, 1 and 3 do not connect to "declines a risky operation".
options: Success rates vary widely between hospitals.
Most patients never read published success rates.
Surgeons generally welcome greater transparency.
But surgeons judged on outcomes may be tempted to avoid the patients most likely to fare badly.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. Translations of sacred texts have often been resisted as threats to the authority of those who could read the original.
  2. When a text can be read only in a learned language, its interpretation remains with a trained few.
  3. A translation into the common tongue allows ordinary readers to judge for themselves.
  4. The disputes over such translations were therefore as much about power as about accuracy.
  5. Some ancient languages survive today only in religious use.
questions.solution: 1-2-3-4 argues that translation threatened interpretive authority, so disputes were about power. Sentence 5 notes the survival of liturgical languages, which is topically related but does not belong to the argument.

questions.question:
Five jumbled sentences related to a topic are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd one out and key in its number.

  1. Wetlands were long regarded as wasteland, fit only to be drained.
  2. They are now valued for absorbing floodwater and filtering pollutants.
  3. Draining them for agriculture was once subsidised by many governments.
  4. Some of those same governments now pay to restore what they paid to destroy.
  5. Drained peat soils can sink by several metres over a century as the organic matter decays.
questions.solution: 1-3-2-4 traces the reversal in attitudes and policy towards wetlands. Sentence 5 describes a physical effect of drainage, on-topic but not part of the reversal in attitudes and policy.

questions.question:
The four sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the four numbers (e.g. 2143).

  1. Each time such a summary was itself summarised, the more surprising details were sharpened and the qualifications dropped.
  2. A study published with careful caveats can become, within a few years, a widely cited fact.
  3. By the time it reached textbooks, the finding had acquired a certainty its authors never claimed.
  4. The process typically begins in summaries written for readers who lack the time to consult the original.
questions.solution: 2 states the phenomenon; 4 ("The process") identifies its start; 1 ("Each time such a summary") continues the process begun in 4 and describes the progression; 3 ("By the time it reached textbooks") concludes it.

questions.question:
The five sentences below, when properly sequenced, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the sequence of the five numbers (e.g. 21435).

  1. Its success, however, depended on a supply of cheap labour that has since disappeared.
  2. For decades the factory town was held up as a model of planned industrial community.
  3. Housing, schools and shops were all provided by the employer, close to the works.
  4. When the labour became expensive, the factory closed and the town lost its reason to exist.
  5. What had looked like a design for living turned out to be a design for a particular economy.
questions.solution: 2 introduces the model; 3 describes it; 1 ("however") introduces the dependency; 4 ("When the labour became expensive") gives the outcome; 5 draws the lesson. 1 needs 3's description before "Its success", and 4 needs 1's "cheap labour".

b16-rc1.title: Telling more than we can know
b16-rc1.html:
Telling more than we can know

Ask people why they chose one of several identical pairs of stockings laid out on a table, and they will give reasons readily: this pair felt softer, that one had a better sheen. In a well-known set of experiments, the pairs really were identical, and the choice was driven mostly by position: people tended to prefer whichever item lay furthest to the right. Yet almost nobody mentioned position, and when it was suggested to them, most denied it firmly. They were not lying. They sincerely believed the reasons they gave.

Findings of this kind have led some psychologists to a startling conclusion: that we have far less direct access to the causes of our own behaviour than we suppose. On this view, when we explain our choices we are not reading off a report from some inner observatory. We are doing what an outsider would do: drawing on a stock of plausible theories about why people act as they do, and applying the one that seems to fit. The tell-tale sign is that our explanations of our own behaviour are often no more accurate than the explanations a stranger would offer for us, and are wrong in the same ways.

It would be easy to overstate the point. The experiments show that people can be mistaken about causes they have no reason to notice, such as the position of an item on a table. They do not show that we are wrong about everything inside us. A person in pain generally knows that she is in pain, and someone working through a sum in her head can usually say which step she is on. What the research undermines is not self-knowledge in general but a particular confidence: the belief that when we can produce a reason for an action, the reason we produce is the one that moved us.

That confidence matters, because so much of social life depends on the reasons people give. We ask job candidates why they want the post, witnesses why they noticed what they did, and voters why they prefer one candidate. If the answers are partly constructions, assembled after the fact from the stock of available theories, then they tell us less about the person than we assume, and more about what that person, and the culture around her, regards as a respectable reason.

There is a further and less comfortable implication. If our explanations are theories, they can be improved, as theories can, but only by evidence that comes from outside. The person who wishes to know why she really avoids certain colleagues may learn more from a careful record of when she does so than from any amount of reflection. Introspection, on this account, is not useless, but it is a source of hypotheses rather than of verdicts, and it deserves the same scepticism we bring to any hypothesis that flatters the person who holds it.

b16-rc2.title: The second life of clothes
b16-rc2.html:
The second life of clothes

Every year, bales of used clothing donated in wealthy countries are sorted, compressed and shipped to markets in East and West Africa, where traders buy them unseen and resell the contents piece by piece. For the donor the transaction ends at the collection bin and feels like charity. For the economies at the other end it is something more complicated: a large, unregulated trade that has been blamed for destroying local textile industries and praised for clothing millions of people cheaply.

The case against the trade is usually made through history. In the decades after independence, several countries built clothing and textile factories that employed tens of thousands of workers. Many of those factories have since closed, and their decline coincided with a flood of imported second-hand clothing. Critics draw the obvious conclusion and some governments have acted on it, proposing high tariffs or outright bans on used garments in the hope of reviving domestic production.

The conclusion is less obvious than it looks. The same decades saw other changes that hurt local factories at least as much: the removal of protective tariffs under structural adjustment programmes, unreliable electricity, and above all the arrival of very cheap new clothing from Asia. Studies that try to separate these causes generally find that second-hand imports played a real but partial role. A ban on used clothing, on this evidence, would be more likely to open the market to cheap new imports than to bring back the old factories.

Meanwhile the trade itself supports a dense web of livelihoods. Importers sell bales to wholesalers, who sell them to market traders, who employ tailors to alter, mend and restyle what they buy. Because no trader knows what a bale contains until it is opened, the business resembles a lottery in which skill lies in judging suppliers, spotting quality and repairing what others would discard. Those who make a living this way are not victims of the trade but its practitioners, and their interests are seldom heard in debates conducted on their behalf.

None of this makes the trade benign. The quality of bales has declined as fast fashion has spread in the donor countries, so that a growing share of what arrives is too worn or too flimsy to sell. That share ends up in landfills and on riverbanks in the importing countries, which bear the cost of disposing of clothes that the donors have, in effect, exported rather than thrown away. The problem here is not that Africans buy used clothes but that rich countries consume clothing at a rate their own waste systems would struggle to absorb.

A useful debate would separate these questions. Whether used clothing harms local industry is an empirical matter, and the answer appears to be: somewhat, but less than other forces. Whether the trade's waste is fair is a question about responsibility, and the answer points back towards the donors' wardrobes rather than towards the markets that receive their castoffs.

b16-rc3.title: The invention of wilderness
b16-rc3.html:
The invention of wilderness

The great national parks of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries were founded on a picture of nature as a place without people. Their creators spoke of untouched landscapes, of country as it had been before human history began, and they drew boundaries to keep it that way. What they seldom acknowledged was that many of these landscapes had been inhabited, hunted, burned and managed for thousands of years, and that making them empty required removing the people who lived there.

Historians have since shown how much of the 'wilderness' that visitors admire is the product of that management. Open grasslands that early travellers took for natural features were often maintained by regular, deliberate burning; when the burning stopped after the inhabitants were expelled, forests crept in and the very scenery the parks had been created to protect began to change. In some places, the removal of grazing or of small-scale cultivation reduced rather than increased the variety of plants and animals.

None of this means that the founders were simply wrong to want to protect these places. The threats they saw, from logging, mining and settlement on an industrial scale, were real, and the parks did save landscapes that would otherwise have been destroyed. The error lay in the idea that protection meant the absence of people, and in the assumption that the people who were there did not count as part of what was being protected.

The idea persists in subtler forms. Conservation funding often flows more readily to projects that promise to keep areas 'intact', a word that quietly implies that human presence is a form of damage. Communities living inside or beside protected areas may be allowed to stay only on condition that they give up practices, such as seasonal burning or the collection of forest produce, that may have helped to shape the habitat in the first place. In such cases, conservation can end up undermining the very ecological conditions it aims to preserve.

The alternative is not to abolish protected areas but to rethink what they are for. If many valued landscapes are joint products of natural processes and long human use, then protecting them may require keeping some of that use going, and the people who know how to do it may be the most useful allies a park can have. Some parks have begun to work in this way, restoring traditional burning under the guidance of the communities that once practised it.

The lesson reaches beyond particular parks. The word 'wilderness' carries a story about human beings as outsiders to nature, visitors who can only spoil what they touch. That story has inspired admirable acts of protection. But a story in which people are always the problem makes it hard to imagine them as part of any solution, and it has fallen hardest on those whose presence in the landscape was longest.

b16-rc4.title: What a tip pays for
b16-rc4.html:
What a tip pays for

Tipping is one of the few economic customs that most of its participants claim to dislike and nearly all continue to practise. In countries where it is expected, diners complain about calculating percentages, workers complain about unpredictable earnings, and economists complain that the custom serves none of the purposes usually claimed for it. Yet attempts by restaurants to abolish tips and raise prices instead have often been abandoned within a year or two.

The standard defence of tipping is that it rewards good service. A waiter who knows that his income depends on the customer's satisfaction will, the argument goes, work harder to provide it. The evidence for this is surprisingly weak. Studies that compare the size of tips with diners' own ratings of the service usually find only a small connection between the two. Tips depend more on the size of the bill, the weather, whether the server introduced herself by name, and the diner's mood than on anything the server did with the food.

If tipping does little to discipline service, why does it survive? One answer is that it disguises prices. A menu without tips must show prices about a fifth higher, and customers comparing menus tend to choose the restaurant that looks cheaper, even when the final bill would be the same. A restaurant that abolishes tipping on its own therefore appears more expensive than its rivals, which is why such experiments have so often failed.

A second answer concerns the relationship between diner and server. Tipping lets the customer feel generous, and turns a commercial payment into something closer to a gift. Many people value that feeling, and some are willing to pay for it. The difficulty is that a gift, unlike a wage, can be withheld, and those who depend on it are exposed to the prejudices as well as the generosity of strangers. Research has repeatedly found that tips vary with servers' appearance, age and ethnicity in ways that have nothing to do with the quality of their work.

These two explanations suggest different remedies. If tipping survives mainly because it hides prices, then the solution lies in rules that require all-inclusive pricing for every restaurant at once, so that no single business is punished for honesty. If it survives because customers value the gesture of giving, then abolition may be neither achievable nor entirely desirable, and the task becomes to limit the damage, for instance by guaranteeing a base wage that does not depend on the gift.

In practice both forces are at work, which may explain why the custom has proved so durable. A practice that conceals prices from customers and offers them a pleasant feeling of generosity at the same time is unlikely to disappear through market pressure alone.

b16-rc5.title: Beauty as evidence
b16-rc5.html:
Beauty as evidence

Physicists often describe the theories they most admire as beautiful, and some have gone further, claiming that beauty is a reliable guide to truth. A theory that explains a wide range of phenomena from a few simple principles, with no arbitrary adjustments, is said to carry a mark of correctness, and history seems to offer support: several equations chosen for their elegance were later confirmed by experiment in ways their authors could not have foreseen.

Sceptics reply that this history is selective. For every elegant theory that was confirmed, there were others, equally admired in their day, that turned out to be false. Nobody remembers them because textbooks record the winners. Moreover, what counts as beautiful has changed. The circular orbits of early astronomy were admired for their perfection, and the ellipses that replaced them were at first thought ugly. If the standard of beauty shifts to accommodate whatever theories succeed, then beauty cannot be an independent test of success.

Defenders of the aesthetic criterion need not claim that beauty guarantees truth. A more modest version holds that, in the absence of decisive evidence, simplicity and economy are reasonable grounds for preferring one theory over another, because a theory with fewer adjustable parts makes sharper predictions and is easier to refute. On this view, elegance is valuable not as a sign that nature itself is beautiful but as a practical virtue: it keeps theories honest by limiting their ability to fit any result.

The difficulty arises when the modest version slides into the ambitious one. In some areas of modern physics, experiments that could decide between rival theories lie far beyond present technology, and may remain so for generations. In that situation it is tempting to let aesthetic judgement do the work of evidence, and to treat a theory's elegance as grounds for believing it rather than merely as grounds for investigating it further. Critics argue that whole research programmes have been sustained for decades in this way, absorbing talent and funding while producing no testable predictions.

The disagreement is not, at bottom, about whether beauty matters. Almost everyone agrees that it guides the choice of which ideas to pursue. It is about what happens when guidance hardens into conviction. A scientist who prefers a simple theory because it is easier to test is using elegance as a tool. A scientist who believes a theory because it is too beautiful to be wrong has made elegance a substitute for the test, and has, in a sense, left science for something closer to taste.

Whether that matters depends on whether the tests eventually arrive. If they do, the beautiful theory will be confirmed or refuted like any other, and the confidence placed in it will be judged by the result. If they never do, the field risks becoming a contest of aesthetic preferences in which the deciding votes belong to whoever holds the most influential positions.

b16-rc6.title: Minds in the sea
b16-rc6.html:
Minds in the sea

The octopus is an awkward animal for anyone who believes that intelligence is a mark of our own lineage. Its last common ancestor with humans was a small, probably worm-like creature that lived more than five hundred million years ago, long before either line had anything resembling a brain. Yet octopuses solve puzzles, use objects as tools, recognise individual people, and appear to play. Whatever intelligence they have, it evolved on its own, by a different route, in a body that could hardly be less like ours.

That body shapes the mind it carries. Most of an octopus's neurons are not in its central brain but in its arms, each of which can taste, touch and respond to what it encounters with a degree of independence. An arm severed from the body will still reach for food and attempt to pass it to a mouth that is no longer there. It is unclear what, if anything, it is like to be such an animal, but it is unlikely to resemble the single, centred point of view that we take for granted in ourselves.

These facts have become practical as well as philosophical. Proposals to farm octopuses on an industrial scale have prompted scientists and ethicists to ask whether the animals can suffer, and if so, what farming would mean for them. A government review in one country concluded that there was strong evidence of sentience in octopuses and their relatives, enough to bring them within animal-welfare law. The evidence included signs that injured octopuses tend their wounds, avoid places where they were hurt, and will accept a painkiller when one is offered.

Critics of the review pointed out that none of these behaviours proves that the animal feels anything. A sufficiently complicated machine might avoid damage and tend its injuries without any experience at all. This is true, but it proves less than the critics hope. The same could be said of any animal other than oneself; we infer that other mammals feel pain from just such behaviour, together with similarities of anatomy. In the octopus the anatomical similarity is missing, which makes the inference weaker, but the behavioural evidence is no less striking.

What, then, should follow from uncertainty? One view holds that we should extend protection only when sentience is established. The opposite view, increasingly influential, holds that when there is a realistic possibility that a creature can suffer, the burden of proof should fall on those who would subject it to conditions likely to cause suffering. The second view does not claim to know what the octopus feels. It claims that ignorance, in a matter where the possible harm is grave and the cost of caution modest, is a reason for restraint rather than a licence.

The octopus thus poses a test less of our science than of our habits of reasoning. We are used to extending moral concern along lines of resemblance. An animal whose mind may be rich but is certainly strange invites us to ask whether resemblance was ever the right guide.

b2-rc1.title: What de-extinction would restore
b2-rc1.html:
What de-extinction would restore

Each time a team of geneticists announces progress towards reviving an extinct animal, the headlines tend to promise a homecoming: the woolly mammoth back on the tundra, the passenger pigeon darkening American skies again. What is actually on offer is more modest and, in some ways, more interesting. No laboratory can recover a complete genome from remains that have lain in permafrost or museum drawers for centuries; DNA breaks into fragments, and the gaps must be filled from living relatives. The likely product is therefore not a mammoth but an elephant edited to carry a few dozen mammoth traits, such as dense hair and a thick layer of fat.

Supporters argue that this distinction matters less than it seems. What an ecosystem notices, they say, is not an animal's pedigree but what it does. If cold-adapted elephants trampled snow and toppled shrubs as mammoths once did, they might help restore the grassland that once covered much of the far north, which, some ecologists argue, keeps the ground beneath it colder than forest does. On this view, de-extinction is a tool for reviving lost ecological functions, and the name is merely a piece of marketing.

Critics accept the functional framing but draw the opposite conclusion from it. If the aim is to restore what an animal did, they ask, why begin with the most expensive and uncertain route? Many lost functions can be partly supplied by species that still exist: horses and bison have been released onto Siberian grassland for exactly this purpose. More pointedly, the money and attention that flow to spectacular revival projects may come at the expense of species that are declining now and could be saved by ordinary means, such as protecting habitat. There is also a worry about moral hazard. If extinction comes to seem reversible, the urgency of preventing it may fade.

Neither side, it should be said, has much evidence to offer yet. No edited animal has yet been set loose in the ecosystem it is meant to restore, so claims about ecological benefit remain projections, and the fear that revival will drain funds from conservation assumes that the money would otherwise have gone there, which is far from certain; much of it comes from private investors drawn by the novelty of the technology itself.

What the debate does reveal is how unclear the goal of conservation has become. For most of its history the field could define success as keeping species from disappearing. Once a species can, in some sense, be rebuilt, that definition no longer settles very much. We are pushed to say what we were trying to preserve all along: particular lineages of living things, the work they did in the world, or our own sense of what a complete landscape looks like.

b2-rc2.title: Why proverbs disagree
b2-rc2.html:
Why proverbs disagree

Collections of proverbs are full of contradictions. 'Look before you leap' sits uneasily beside 'he who hesitates is lost'; 'many hands make light work' is flatly denied by 'too many cooks spoil the broth'. To the systematic mind this looks like an embarrassment. A body of advice that recommends both caution and boldness, both cooperation and its avoidance, seems to recommend nothing at all.

The embarrassment fades once we ask what proverbs are for. They are not premises from which conclusions can be deduced, still less laws that hold in all cases. They are closer to tools, each suited to a recurring kind of situation.
