A carpenter is not inconsistent for owning both a saw and a glue pot; the question is never which tool is correct in general, but which one this job needs. A proverb is summoned when a speaker has already sized up a situation and wants to name it compactly, and the name carries a recommendation with it. The recommendation is only as good as the sizing-up that came before it: describe a hasty plan as bold and the proverb about hesitation blesses it; describe it as reckless and the proverb about looking first condemns it.

This means that the real knowledge lies not in the proverbs but in the judgement that selects among them, and that judgement is precisely what proverbs cannot supply. No proverb tells you whether the moment calls for looking or for leaping. Seen in this light, the oddity is not that proverbs contradict each other but that anyone expected them not to. A culture that offered only one of each pair would be giving worse advice, not better, because it would be pretending that one kind of situation never occurs.

There is, however, a less flattering side to this flexibility. Because a proverb can be found to support almost any course of action, proverbs are well suited to justifying decisions after they have been made. The person who rushed in and succeeded quotes the saying about hesitation; had the venture failed, an onlooker would have been ready with the one about looking first. Used this way, the stock of proverbs becomes a device for making every outcome seem to have been foreseeable.

The two uses are hard to tell apart from the outside, since the same words serve both. The difference lies in timing and in honesty: whether the saying is brought to the situation before the choice, as a way of thinking about it, or fitted to the result afterwards, as a way of not having to. A simple test is to ask whether the speaker could have said in advance which saying they would reach for. If so, the proverb did some work; if the choice was settled only by how things turned out, it did none.

cv-luck.title: Passage: Moral luck
cv-luck.html:
Passage: Moral luck

Imagine two drivers who leave the same party, each having had a glass of wine too many. Both drive home along similar roads with the same degree of carelessness. On the first driver's route, nothing happens. On the second's, a child runs into the street, and the car cannot stop in time. Most of us judge the second driver far more harshly than the first; the law does too, imposing penalties of an entirely different order. Yet the two drivers did exactly the same thing. The only difference between them lies in something neither controlled: whether a child happened to step off the kerb.

Philosophers call this phenomenon moral luck, and the phrase is meant to sound uncomfortable. A widely shared intuition holds that we should be praised or blamed only for what is within our control. The careless drivers controlled how much they drank and whether they chose to drive, but not who crossed their path. If that intuition is right, then the two drivers deserve exactly the same blame, and our harsher verdict on the second is a kind of mistake.

The difficulty is that the control principle, applied consistently, threatens to swallow almost everything. We do not control the temperament we are born with, the upbringing that shaped our values, or the circumstances that test them. A person who would have collaborated with a tyrannical regime, had they lived under one, may live a blameless life simply because they were born elsewhere. If we strip away everything that luck has touched, it is not obvious that anything remains to be judged at all.

Some thinkers have responded by biting the bullet: moral assessment, they say, should attach only to the inner will, to intentions and choices, and outcomes are morally irrelevant. This view has the merit of consistency, but it struggles to explain experiences that seem central to moral life. The second driver will rightly feel something the first does not, a particular kind of regret that is more than mere sadness that a bad thing occurred. To tell him that his feelings rest on a confusion seems not merely unkind but false to what has happened.

Others argue that the right response is not to abolish moral luck but to accept it as a feature of our condition. On this view, we are not disembodied wills floating free of the world; we are agents whose actions spill into consequences we cannot fully foresee, and taking responsibility means owning those consequences, including the unlucky ones. The price of this acceptance is that morality becomes less tidy and, in a sense, less fair. But perhaps the demand that morality be perfectly fair was itself a fantasy, born of the hope that we could stand outside the world we act in.

cv-repair.title: Passage: The price of repair
cv-repair.html:
Passage: The price of repair

For most of the twentieth century, a broken household object presented its owner with a simple calculation. A toaster, a radio or a pair of shoes was expensive relative to wages, while the labour needed to mend it was cheap. Repair shops lined the streets of every town, and the decision to fix rather than replace was so obvious that it hardly felt like a decision at all. Over the past few decades that arithmetic has quietly inverted. Manufacturing has become so efficient, and global supply chains so long, that a new appliance can cost less than an hour of a skilled technician's time. The repair shop has not been defeated by consumer laziness; it has been priced out.

Economists recognise this as a version of what is called the 'cost disease'. In sectors where productivity rises quickly, such as manufacturing, prices tend to fall; in sectors where it barely moves, such as hands-on services, wages must still keep pace with the rest of the economy, so prices rise. Repair belongs firmly to the second group. A technician diagnosing a faulty washing machine today works at roughly the same speed as one did fifty years ago, yet must be paid a modern wage. The relative price of fixing things therefore climbs year after year, regardless of anyone's intentions.

This framing matters because it changes what a sensible policy response looks like. If throwing things away were merely a cultural failing, the remedy would be exhortation: campaigns urging people to value what they own. But if the problem is mainly one of relative prices, moral appeals will achieve little. People respond to the costs in front of them, and most households cannot afford to pay more to keep an old machine running than to buy a new one, however virtuous that choice might be.

The more promising interventions therefore target the price gap directly. Some governments have experimented with lowering taxes on repair services, or with requiring manufacturers to sell spare parts and publish repair manuals for a set number of years. These right-to-repair rules are often described as consumer-protection measures, but their deeper effect is economic: by making parts available and designs easier to open, they reduce the hours a technician must spend on each job, and so attack the very cost that made repair uncompetitive.

None of this means that culture is irrelevant. Habits formed when repair was impractical can persist long after the economics improves, and a generation that has never had an object mended may not think to ask. But culture tends to follow prices more readily than it leads them. A society that wants its citizens to repair more would do better to make repair cheaper than to make them feel guilty.

cv-replication.title: Passage: The replication crisis
cv-replication.html:
Passage: The replication crisis

In the early 2010s, researchers in several fields began to confront an awkward possibility: that a substantial share of published findings might not hold up if the studies were simply run again. Large collaborative efforts set out to repeat well-known experiments in psychology, and later in economics and cancer biology, following the original methods as closely as possible. The results were sobering. In several of these projects, fewer than half of the repeated studies produced effects as strong as the originals, and some effects vanished altogether. The episode came to be known as the replication crisis.

It would be easy to read this as a story of fraud, but deliberate fabrication explains only a small part of it. The deeper causes are structural. Journals have long preferred to publish striking, positive results over null findings, and careers depend on publications. Under these pressures, researchers face many small decisions that seem individually harmless: which outliers to exclude, which of several measures to report, when to stop collecting data. Each choice can nudge a result across the conventional threshold of statistical significance. Taken together, such choices can make chance patterns look like real discoveries, even when no one intends to deceive.

The statistical threshold itself has come in for criticism. A result is conventionally called significant if, assuming there were no real effect, data at least as extreme would arise less than five per cent of the time. This is often misread as meaning that there is only a five per cent chance the finding is false. In reality, the probability that a significant result reflects a true effect depends heavily on how plausible the hypothesis was to begin with and on how much statistical power the study had. When many long-shot hypotheses are tested in small samples, a large fraction of the significant results can be false alarms.

Reformers have proposed a range of remedies. One of the most influential is preregistration, in which researchers publicly record their hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting data, so that later choices cannot be shaped by the results. Another is the registered report, a format in which a journal agrees to publish a study on the strength of its design, before the results are known, removing the incentive to produce a striking outcome. Larger samples, shared data and routine replication have also gained ground.

Some critics worry that these reforms may stifle exploratory research, the open-ended poking around that often precedes genuine breakthroughs. The reformers' usual reply is that exploration is welcome, provided it is labelled as such. The aim is not to forbid researchers from following hunches, but to stop hunches confirmed after the fact from being presented as predictions made in advance.

cv-translation.title: Passage: Translating poetry
cv-translation.html:
Passage: Translating poetry

There is an old quip that poetry is what gets lost in translation. Like most quips, it contains a truth wrapped in an exaggeration. A poem is not simply a set of statements that could be restated in other words; it is a particular arrangement of sounds, rhythms and associations that belong to one language and no other. When a line in Urdu or Tamil depends on a word that means two things at once, or on a rhyme that exists only in that tongue, the translator faces a choice in which something must be given up.

Translators have broadly divided into two camps over how to make that sacrifice. The first holds that fidelity to meaning comes first: the translator's task is to carry across what the poem says, as precisely as possible, even if the result reads stiffly. The second argues that a poem which no longer works as a poem has not been translated at all, only paraphrased. For this camp, the translator must be willing to invent, to substitute a new rhyme or image that produces in the reader something like the effect the original produced in its first audience.

Each position has its characteristic failure. Strict fidelity can yield texts that are accurate in every particular and lifeless as a whole, like a pressed flower that preserves the shape of a bloom but none of its scent. Free recreation, on the other hand, risks replacing the original poet with the translator, so that readers praise a voice that was never really there. Some celebrated translations are admired precisely as poems in their own right, which is both a tribute to the translator and a quiet admission of distance from the source.

A third approach refuses to choose. Some translators publish the original alongside a literal version and a freer rendering, inviting readers to triangulate between them. Others add notes explaining the puns and allusions that could not survive the crossing. These methods ask more of the reader, but they treat the loss honestly rather than disguising it.

Perhaps the most useful way to see the problem is to abandon the idea that a translation could ever be a replacement for the original. A translation is better understood as a reading: one person's careful, partial and inevitably personal account of what a poem is and does. Seen this way, the existence of many competing translations is not a sign that the task has failed, but evidence of the poem's richness. Each version catches a different facet, and no single version, however skilled, can catch them all.

ez-rc1.title: Passage: How railways set the clock
ez-rc1.html:
Passage: How railways set the clock

Until the middle of the nineteenth century, every town kept its own time. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest over the local church or town hall, and clocks were set by it. Because the sun appears to move from east to west, a town a few hundred kilometres to the west reached noon several minutes later than its neighbour. For most people this hardly mattered. A farmer walking to market did not care whether his clock agreed with one in a distant city.

The railways changed that. A train could now cover in a morning a distance that once took days, and its timetable had to be read by passengers at many stations. If each station printed departures in its own local time, the same train seemed to leave at odd and confusing minutes, and travellers who changed lines often missed their connections. Worse, railway staff working on single-track lines relied on timetables to keep trains apart. A disagreement of a few minutes between two stations could put two engines on the same stretch of track.

Railway companies responded by choosing one time for the whole network, usually the time at a major city, and telling every station to follow it. In Britain this 'railway time' spread quickly in the 1840s, carried along the telegraph wires that ran beside the tracks. Some towns resisted at first. A few public clocks were fitted with two minute hands, one for local time and one for the railway, so that citizens could see what they were giving up. Within a generation, however, the convenience of a single time won, and the law eventually followed the practice.

Larger countries faced a harder problem, because one time across a whole continent would put noon in the middle of the night somewhere. The answer, agreed in stages during the late nineteenth century, was to divide the world into zones, each usually one hour apart. Inside a zone, clocks agree; crossing into the next zone, travellers simply move their watches forward or back by an hour.

Time zones now feel so natural that it is easy to forget they were invented for a practical reason. They were not handed down by astronomers seeking accuracy. If anything, they made clocks less faithful to the local sun. They were a compromise, accepted because a society that moves quickly needs its members to agree on what time it is, even if that agreed time is slightly wrong for the place where they stand.

ez-rc2.title: Passage: Trees on city streets
ez-rc2.html:
Passage: Trees on city streets

Walk down a city street on a hot afternoon and you can feel the difference a row of trees makes. Measurements in many cities show that shaded pavements can be several degrees cooler than exposed ones, and the air under a dense canopy is noticeably more comfortable. Trees cool a street in two ways. Their leaves block sunlight before it can heat the road and walls, and they release water vapour, which carries heat away as it evaporates.

The benefits do not stop at temperature. Tree roots and the soil around them soak up rainwater that would otherwise rush into drains, which helps during heavy storms. Leaves trap some dust from traffic. Studies of shopping streets have found that people tend to linger longer where there is greenery, which is good news for small shops. There is also evidence that residents of leafy neighbourhoods report less stress, though such findings are harder to measure precisely. Birds and insects also find food and shelter in street trees, so a well-planted avenue can link small parks into a chain of green space across the city.

Yet street trees lead difficult lives. Their roots are squeezed between pipes, cables and foundations, and the soil beneath a pavement is often packed so hard that water and air cannot reach them. Many young trees planted with great ceremony die within a few years because nobody waters them during their first dry seasons. Others are cut back severely when they grow into overhead wires or block shop signs. A tree that survives all this may still be removed when a road is widened.

For these reasons, experts increasingly argue that the number of trees planted is a poor measure of success. A city that plants a thousand saplings and loses most of them has achieved little. What matters is how many trees reach maturity, because a large old tree provides many times the shade and water absorption of a young one. This shifts attention from planting days to less glamorous work: preparing good soil pits, choosing species that suit local conditions, and paying crews to water and inspect trees for years afterwards.

None of this is especially costly compared with other city spending, but it requires patience. The rewards of a tree arrive slowly, often after the officials who planted it have left office. Cities that have built lasting canopies tend to be those that treated trees as long-term public infrastructure, like water pipes or roads, rather than as decorations to be added for a ribbon-cutting.

ez-rc3.title: Passage: What libraries are for now
ez-rc3.html:
Passage: What libraries are for now

When home internet connections became common, many people predicted that public libraries would fade away. If any fact could be found on a phone in seconds, why would anyone visit a building full of books? Some local governments acted on this belief and cut library budgets, shortened opening hours or closed branches altogether. The prediction seemed reasonable. It turned out to misunderstand what libraries actually do.

Libraries have never been only stores of information. They are also among the few indoor public places where a person can stay for hours without being expected to buy anything. Students without a quiet room at home use them to study. Elderly residents come for newspapers and company. Parents bring small children to story sessions, often the child's first experience of a group activity outside the family. Job seekers use library computers and printers to prepare applications, and many people still need help from a librarian to fill in an online form. On a cold or very hot day, a library may also be the only comfortable public room nearby. For people living alone, a short conversation at the front desk can be the main social contact of the week.

In fact, the internet has created new reasons to visit. Government services, banking and even school homework have moved online, but not everyone has a reliable connection, a working computer or the confidence to use them. For these people the library is the bridge. Librarians in many towns report that they spend less time finding books and more time helping visitors with passwords, email accounts and digital forms.

Libraries that have thrived tend to be those that recognised this shift. They have rearranged their spaces, adding study rooms, meeting areas and workshops alongside the shelves. Some lend tools, musical instruments or laptops. Others host classes in everything from basic computing to tax filing. Books remain central, and borrowing figures for children's books in particular have held up well, but they are no longer the whole story.

None of this means that libraries are safe. They depend on public funding, and their benefits are spread across many people in small amounts, which makes them easy to cut when budgets are tight. But the early prediction of their disappearance was based on a narrow view of their purpose. A library is less a warehouse of books than a shared room open to everyone, and the need for such rooms has not gone away.

ez-rc4.title: Passage: The coast's living wall
ez-rc4.html:
Passage: The coast's living wall

Along many tropical coasts, the boundary between land and sea is not a beach but a forest. Mangroves are trees that have adapted to grow in salty, waterlogged mud that would kill most plants. Some send up small breathing roots from the mud, because the soil itself contains so little oxygen. Others stand on arching roots that look like stilts, holding the trunk above the rising and falling tide. Twice a day, the sea flows in among their roots and drains out again. Their leaves can get rid of extra salt, and some species simply keep it out at the roots. These adaptations let mangroves live where few other trees can compete with them.

For a long time, mangroves were treated as wasteland. They were difficult to walk through, full of mosquitoes and of little obvious use, so they were cleared for shrimp ponds, ports and housing. Large areas disappeared in the second half of the twentieth century. Only gradually did people come to see what had been lost.

The tangled roots that make mangroves hard to cross are exactly what makes them valuable. They slow down waves and trap mud, so the coast behind them erodes more slowly. During storms, a wide belt of mangroves can reduce the height and force of the water that reaches villages further inland. The calm, shaded water among the roots is also a nursery for young fish, crabs and prawns, many of which later move out to sea, where fishermen catch them. In this way, cutting a mangrove forest can reduce fish catches far from the place where the trees once stood.

Mangroves also store large amounts of carbon, mostly in the deep mud beneath them rather than in the trees themselves. Because the mud is waterlogged, dead plant material breaks down very slowly and can stay buried for centuries. When mangroves are cleared and the mud dries out, much of this carbon is released into the air.

Many countries now protect their remaining mangroves and try to replant lost ones. Replanting has had mixed results. Seedlings placed in the wrong part of the shore, where the tide is too deep or too shallow, often die. The most successful projects tend to start by restoring the natural flow of water, after which mangroves often return on their own. The lesson is a familiar one in conservation: it is usually easier and cheaper to keep a healthy ecosystem than to rebuild one.

ez-rc5.title: Passage: Why we keep a spare key
ez-rc5.html:
Passage: Why we keep a spare key

Most households keep a spare key somewhere: with a neighbour, under a flowerpot, or in a drawer at a relative's house. The spare is rarely used. Yet people who lose their only key, and spend an evening waiting for a locksmith, tend to make a spare the very next day. The spare key is a small example of a larger idea that engineers call redundancy: having more than one way of doing something important, so that a single failure does not stop everything.

Redundancy is everywhere in systems that must not fail. Aircraft have more than one engine and several independent ways of controlling the wings. Hospitals keep generators in case the electricity supply is cut. Large websites copy their data onto machines in different cities. In each case, the extra part sits idle most of the time, and an accountant looking only at everyday costs might call it waste. The value of the spare shows only in the rare moment when the main part fails. Then the backup takes over, often so smoothly that passengers, patients or users never notice that anything went wrong.

That is exactly the temptation organisations face. When budgets are tight, spare capacity is an easy target. A factory can save money by holding less stock in its warehouse and relying on deliveries arriving just in time. A team can work with no extra staff, so that everyone is fully busy. In normal times these choices look efficient. The cost appears only when something goes wrong: a delivery is delayed, a worker falls ill, and there is nothing in reserve to absorb the shock.

This does not mean that more redundancy is always better. Every spare costs money, takes space and must be maintained. A spare generator that has never been tested may fail on the one day it is needed. The skill lies in deciding which failures would be serious enough to justify a backup, and in checking that the backup really works.

The spare key captures this balance well. It is cheap, and the trouble it saves is large, so almost everyone agrees it is worth having. But it only helps if someone remembers where it is and if it still fits the lock. Good redundancy, in a household or a hospital, is not just a matter of owning a spare. It means keeping that spare ready for the day it is needed.

m1-rc1.title: Passage: The economics of the queue
m1-rc1.html:
Passage: The economics of the queue

A queue is usually described as a failure: a sign that a price was set too low or that a supplier could not keep up. Economists in particular tend to see the line outside a bakery or a passport office as wasted hours that a better price would have abolished. If people are willing to stand for forty minutes, the argument runs, they would surely have paid something instead, and that payment could have funded more counters or more ovens.

The argument is tidy, but it assumes that money and time are interchangeable for everyone at the same rate. They are not. An hour is worth very different amounts to a surgeon and to a retired clerk, yet each owns exactly twenty-four of them a day. A queue, unlike a price, charges every participant in a currency that is distributed with rough equality. That is why queues persist for goods that communities regard as matters of fairness rather than of commerce: emergency care, public housing, seats at a free concert in the park.

None of this makes queues efficient. The person who most needs a service is not always the one with the most time to spare, and the hours spent waiting produce nothing for anyone. Some queues also quietly reintroduce money, as when people hire others to stand in line for them. Once that happens, the queue no longer rations by time; it rations by the wages of the stand-ins, and its claim to fairness collapses.

What the queue offers, then, is not efficiency but legibility. Everyone can see the line, judge its length and understand why the person at the front is served first. A price that clears the market silently may allocate goods more productively, but it does so out of view, and those who are excluded are rarely told why. Public institutions that replace queues with fees often discover that the resentment they provoke is less about the money than about the loss of a rule anyone could follow.

Consider what happens when a queue is replaced. A city that auctions its scarce housing permits, or sells priority access to a public clinic, does not abolish rationing; it changes the currency in which the rationing is paid. Those who lose under the new rule are rarely persuaded by the observation that total waiting time has fallen. They notice instead that a good once available to anyone willing to stand in line is now available to anyone willing to pay, and they suspect, often correctly, that the people who were willing to pay were not the people who were standing. Economists can answer that the revenue might be used to compensate the losers. The answer is sound on paper and almost never realised in practice, because the compensation is diffuse, delayed and invisible, while the exclusion is immediate and personal.

The queue also disciplines those who manage it in a way a price does not. A line that grows longer every week is a public accusation, visible to journalists and to the officials who must walk past it; a price that rises quietly to match demand produces no such scene.

The more useful question, therefore, is not whether a queue wastes time, which it plainly does, but whether the good being rationed is one for which a community values a visible and equal rule more than the time it costs. Where the answer is yes, shortening the queue is a better reform than abolishing it.

m1-rc2.title: Passage: Assisted migration of trees
m1-rc2.html:
Passage: Assisted migration of trees

Forests move, but slowly. After the last glaciation, many tree species in the northern temperate zone expanded their ranges by a few hundred metres a year, carried by birds, rodents and wind. The climate now projected for this century is expected to shift suitable conditions far faster than that, and a growing number of foresters argue that trees will need help. Their proposal, usually called assisted migration, is to plant seed from warmer, lower or more southerly populations in places where the climate is expected to resemble those origins within a few decades.

The case in favour is straightforward. A tree planted today may live for a century or more, so it must be suited not to the present climate of its site but to the climates it will meet over its life. Seed collected locally is adapted to a past that will not return. Planting it is, on this view, the riskier choice, though it looks like caution.

Critics raise two kinds of objection. The first concerns forecasting. Climate models agree on broad trends but differ on regional rainfall, the frequency of late frosts and the timing of droughts, and it is precisely these details that decide whether a seedling survives. A population moved to match a forecast average may be killed by an extreme the forecast smoothed away. The second objection concerns what travels with the seed. Fungi, insects and microbial partners do not always come along, and those that do may meet local relatives with which they have never coexisted.

Proponents reply that the first objection argues for diversity rather than inaction: plant a mixture of origins, so that whatever climate arrives, some fraction is suited to it. This answer is attractive but it quietly changes the goal. A mixed planting is no longer an attempt to put the right tree in the right place; it is a hedge against not knowing which tree is right. That may well be wise, but it means accepting a lower expected growth in exchange for a lower risk of total loss, and it makes the forest an insurance portfolio as much as an ecosystem.

The forecasting objection also has a practical edge that is rarely spelled out. Seed moved several hundred kilometres to suit a warmer future must survive the present climate first, including the hard winters that a warming trend does not abolish. A sapling chosen for the conditions of 2080 may be killed by a frost in 2030, long before the climate it was selected for arrives. Foresters thus face a choice between material suited to the start of a tree's life and material suited to its end, and no single origin is likely to be well suited to both.

The second objection is harder to answer, because its costs, if they arrive, are not confined to the plantation. A forester can choose to accept risk for her own stand; she cannot easily make that choice on behalf of the surrounding woodland.

m1-rc3.title: Passage: Patina and the restorer
m1-rc3.html:
Passage: Patina and the restorer

When a restorer cleans a painted ceiling, the public usually expects to be shown something lost: colours brighter than anyone living has seen, figures sharper than the photographs in guidebooks. The unveiling is staged as a recovery. But the restorer's actual decisions are less like recovery and more like editing, because the layer removed is not simply dirt. It contains soot and varnish, certainly, but also the retouchings of earlier restorers, glazes the artist may have added late, and the slow chemical changes of the paint itself.

Some restorers adopt the rule of removing everything that was not applied by the original hand. The rule sounds objective, yet it requires a judgement about what the original hand applied, and that judgement often rests on the very technical analysis whose interpretation is in dispute. A thin brown layer may be a later varnish or a finishing glaze; the instruments can tell us its composition, not its intention.

Others argue for preserving patina, the accumulated surface of age, on the grounds that the work we inherit is a historical object and not merely an artist's plan. On this view a ceiling darkened by three centuries of candles tells the truth about its life, and a cleaned ceiling tells a pleasing story about its birth. This position has its own difficulty. Patina is not neutral either; it can obscure details the artist plainly meant to be seen and can create effects of mood that viewers then attribute to the painter.

The difficulty is sharpened by the fact that restorers' own materials age. Retouchings made in one generation to fill losses were often chosen to match the painting as it then appeared, darkened and yellowed; when a later team removes the grime, those retouchings stand out as dull patches and must themselves be removed or redone. Several celebrated campaigns of the last century are now being partly reversed by restorers who regard them as heavy-handed, and it would be naive to suppose that present work will escape the same fate. A cleaning is therefore not a final act but an episode in a sequence, and each episode removes material that later restorers can no longer consult.

This has led some institutions to adopt a principle of reversibility: nothing should be added that cannot later be taken away. The principle is sensible for additions but says nothing about removal, which is the more consequential part of any cleaning. Varnish once dissolved, or a glaze mistaken for dirt, cannot be put back. The decisive question in restoration is therefore rarely what to apply, and almost always what to take away, and on that question the available rules give less guidance than their confident language suggests.

What neither rule escapes is that every cleaning produces a new object that has never existed before: not the painting as first seen, which cannot be recovered, nor the painting as last seen, which has been altered. The honest course may be to stop presenting restorations as revelations. A restorer who publishes what was removed, why, and on what evidence turns the unveiling from a claim of truth into an argument that others can examine.

m1-rc4.title: Passage: Regret as evidence
m1-rc4.html:
Passage: Regret as evidence

It is often said that regret is irrational: the past cannot be changed, so suffering over it wastes energy that could be spent on the future. The advice has the appeal of good sense, and in its practical form, do not dwell, it is often sound. As a claim about what regret is, however, it misdescribes the emotion. Regret is not primarily an attempt to change the past. It is a judgement, felt rather than stated, that one's past choice was worse than an available alternative, by the lights of values one still holds.

Read this way, regret carries information. If I regret a harsh word to a friend, my regret tells me, and can tell others, that I still value the friendship and accept that I fell short of a standard I endorse. The absence of regret in such a case would be the more troubling sign. A person who felt nothing would either not hold the value or not see that he had violated it. The emotion is thus not irrational but answerable to reasons: it can be appropriate or inappropriate, proportionate or excessive, as a belief can be true or false.

It helps to distinguish regret from two states it is often confused with. Disappointment concerns outcomes that were not in our control: I can be disappointed by the weather or by a friend's decision, but I cannot strictly regret either. Remorse, at the other extreme, concerns wrongs done to others and carries a demand for repair. Regret occupies the ground between them. It concerns choices that were ours, measured against standards we hold, whether or not anyone else was harmed. A person may regret wasting a talent without having wronged anyone, and that regret is no less a judgement for being private.

Seen in this light, the practical advice not to dwell is advice about the management of a judgement, not a refutation of it. One may decide that a regret has done its work, that its lesson has been absorbed and that further attention to it would be self-indulgent, without concluding that the regret was mistaken in the first place.

This has an awkward consequence. If regret is a judgement relative to values, then a change of values can change what it is rational to regret, without any new facts about the past. Someone who once regretted leaving a secure job for an uncertain art may, years later and with different priorities, find the regret dissolving, not because she has learned anything new about the job, but because she now weighs security differently. The past act is unchanged; its standing in her life is not.

Some find this troubling, as though it made the meaning of our histories hostage to our moods. But values are not moods. They are relatively stable commitments that we revise slowly and, when we are careful, for reasons. That our assessment of the past should shift when such commitments shift is no more scandalous than that a historian's judgement of an era should change when she comes to care about questions her predecessors ignored. What would be irrational is regret that tracked no value at all, or a value one has openly abandoned.

m2-rc1.title: Passage: Why museums repatriate slowly
m2-rc1.html:
Passage: Why museums repatriate slowly

Requests to return objects held in museums are often presented as a contest between two simple positions. On one side stand the claimants, who say the objects were taken under conditions that no one would now accept; on the other stand the museums, which are said to cling to their collections out of pride or commercial interest. The real obstacles are usually less dramatic and more stubborn.

The first is documentary. A museum may hold an object for a century without knowing exactly how it was acquired. Records were kept for insurance and display, not for the questions now being asked of them, and a single line in a ledger — "purchased from a dealer, 1911" — can hide anything from an honest sale to the resale of looted goods. Establishing what happened requires research that is slow, expensive and frequently inconclusive.

The second obstacle is legal. In many countries, objects in national museums belong to the state and may be removed from the collection only by an act of the legislature. Curators who are personally persuaded that an object should go home may be forbidden from sending it. Critics who treat every delay as evidence of bad faith misread this situation; the people they are addressing often lack the power to say yes.

The third obstacle is the most awkward to state openly. A claim implies a claimant, and it is not always clear who that is. A carving made by a community that later split, moved or was absorbed into a modern state may be sought by more than one party, each with a plausible connection to it. A museum that returns the object to one of them may find that it has taken sides in a dispute it barely understands.

Each obstacle also interacts with the others. Uncertain records make legislators reluctant to act, since a law authorising a return must name what is being returned and why; and the existence of several plausible claimants gives legislators a respectable reason to wait until the claimants agree among themselves, which they may never do. A museum that wishes to move quickly may therefore find itself waiting on a parliament that is waiting on a dispute it has no power to resolve.

Some institutions have tried to escape this circle by separating the question of ownership from the question of custody. An object may be legally transferred while remaining on loan to the museum that held it, or physically returned while title remains unresolved. Such arrangements are untidy and satisfy neither side completely, but they allow something to happen while the slower questions are worked out.

None of this means that museums should be left to proceed at their own pace. Documentary uncertainty can be used as an excuse for indefinite delay, and legal restrictions are themselves choices that legislatures can revisit. But a debate that treats repatriation as a test of moral courage alone will keep producing frustration, because it directs its pressure at the wrong people and ignores the questions that actually take time to answer.

m2-rc2.title: Passage: The memory of water tables
m2-rc2.html:
Passage: The memory of water tables

A well that has served a village for generations can fail within a few dry years, and the usual explanation is that the rains stopped. Often the rains have merely become less regular, and the failure has more to do with what happened decades earlier. Groundwater responds to change slowly. Water that falls on a hillside today may take years or centuries to reach the aquifer that a distant pump draws upon, so the level in a well is a kind of delayed record of past rainfall and past use.

This delay creates a peculiar problem for those who manage water. When pumping begins in a region, the water table may barely move for years, because the aquifer is drawing on stored water that took a long time to accumulate. Officials who watch the level conclude, reasonably enough, that extraction is sustainable. By the time the decline becomes visible, the volume being withdrawn has usually grown, more wells have been sunk, and livelihoods depend on them. Reducing extraction then means imposing a loss on people who were never warned.

The same delay works in the other direction. A region that cuts its pumping may see no recovery for years, and the patience required to persist with an unpopular policy that shows no results is rarely available to elected officials. Recharge schemes that slow runoff and let water seep into the ground face the same handicap: their benefits arrive after the people who paid for them have stopped paying attention.

The difficulty is compounded by the way groundwater is commonly held. In many places the water beneath a farm is treated as belonging to whoever sinks a well on it, so that each farmer's pumping lowers the water available to every neighbour without any record of who took what. Deeper and more powerful pumps allow the better-capitalised farmers to follow the falling water down, while their neighbours' shallow wells run dry first. The early signs of depletion therefore appear as the misfortune of particular households, attributed to bad luck or poor equipment, rather than as a regional fact that calls for a regional response. By the time the pattern is recognised, the farmers who could afford to dig deeper have every reason to resist limits that would fall on the water only they can still reach.

Hydrologists have tools to estimate these lags, but the estimates are uncertain, and uncertainty tends to be resolved in favour of present use. A projection that the aquifer might fail in twenty years or might last for sixty is read as permission to continue. What is lacking is less information than an institution capable of acting on information whose consequences will fall on a later generation of users. Some regions have experimented with assigning each user a share of the aquifer's estimated safe yield, so that restraint is not a gift to one's neighbours but a protection of one's own entitlement. The results are mixed, but the approach at least aligns the time horizon of the individual with that of the resource.

m2-rc3.title: Passage: Translation and the untranslatable
m2-rc3.html:
Passage: Translation and the untranslatable

It has become a commonplace that some words cannot be translated. Lists circulate of terms from various languages — a word for the particular light of late afternoon, another for the sadness of a place one has left — offered as proof that each language carves the world in its own way. The lists are charming, but the conclusion drawn from them is weaker than it looks.

That a language has a single word for something does not show that speakers of other languages cannot think it. The very lists that celebrate untranslatable words translate them, usually in a phrase or a sentence, and readers understand the explanation well enough to enjoy it. What is missing in the second language is not the concept but its compression: a ready-made unit that can be used without explanation. That difference is real. A compressed concept can be invoked quickly, combined with others, and passed on without effort, and over time it may come to seem more natural to those who have it. But a difference in convenience is not a difference in what can be thought.

The more serious difficulty for translators lies elsewhere. A word in a living language carries associations from its uses — the poems it has appeared in, the jokes it has served, the registers in which it is polite or rude. A translator can render the meaning of a sentence and lose all of these, or preserve some of them at the cost of the plain sense. This is not a problem of single words but of whole texts, and it arises with ordinary vocabulary as much as with exotic terms. The word for "home" in one language may be bureaucratic in tone; its nearest equivalent in another may be tender.

Register makes the point clearly. Many languages distinguish between forms of address for intimates and for strangers, and the choice between them can carry a story of its own: a shift from the formal to the familiar in the middle of a conversation may mark a seduction, an insult or a reconciliation. A language that lacks the distinction cannot reproduce the shift with a single word. The translator must either signal it some other way, by a change in tone or an added gesture, or let it pass, accepting that a reader of the translation will miss a moment that any reader of the original would notice at once. Neither choice is a failure of understanding; both are decisions about which losses a particular text can bear.

The same is true of words that have been used by a famous writer. Once a poet has made a word her own, every later use of it carries a faint echo of hers for readers who know the poem, and that echo cannot travel into another language unless the poem has travelled with it.

Seen this way, the popular lists mislead in two directions. They exaggerate the gulf between languages at the level of concepts, where explanation can bridge most gaps, and they understate it at the level of texture, where a translation can be accurate in every sentence and still feel like a different work.

m2-rc4.title: Passage: Benchmarks and what they reward
m2-rc4.html:
Passage: Benchmarks and what they reward

Every field that measures progress by a shared benchmark eventually learns the same lesson: the benchmark begins as a proxy for what people care about and ends as the thing they care about. A test set of images, a standard corpus of questions, a reference chip design — each is adopted because it is convenient, public and stable, which allows results from different laboratories to be compared. These virtues are real. Before benchmarks, claims of improvement were often impossible to check.

The difficulty is that stability, the benchmark's chief virtue, is also the source of its decay. Once a test stays fixed, the community's methods gradually adapt to its quirks. No one need cheat. Thousands of researchers each try many variations, publish those that score best, and build on the published work of others. The collective search finds whatever regularities the test happens to contain, including ones unrelated to the general ability it was meant to measure. Scores rise steadily; whether the underlying capability has risen as much is harder to tell.

The obvious response is to replace benchmarks often, and some communities do. But frequent replacement sacrifices comparability, which was the point of the exercise, and each new benchmark tends to be built by people whose sense of what is difficult has itself been shaped by the old one. A subtler response is to treat improvement on a fixed benchmark as evidence that must be corroborated elsewhere — on data gathered later, in other settings, by other people — before it is believed. This is slower and less glamorous than announcing a new record, and it fits poorly with the incentives of publication.

The effect is magnified by the way results are published. A method that improves the benchmark score by a fraction of a point is publishable; one that performs no better on the benchmark but is cheaper, more robust or easier to understand often is not. Over time the field's collective attention narrows to the dimension the benchmark measures, and properties that matter in practice but are not scored, such as the cost of running a system or its behaviour on unfamiliar inputs, receive less effort than they deserve. Reviewers are not to blame for this; a shared number is the easiest thing to agree on when time is short and submissions are many. But the ease is itself part of the problem, because it allows a community to substitute agreement about a score for agreement about what the score was meant to indicate.

It would be wrong to conclude that benchmarks are a mistake. Fields without them tend to drift into a different failure, in which each group evaluates its own methods on its own data and progress becomes a matter of persuasion. The choice is not between measuring and not measuring but between measures whose limits are acknowledged and measures that are treated as the goal itself.

m3-rc1.title: Passage: The paradox of choice in public services
m3-rc1.html:
Passage: The paradox of choice in public services

Reformers who wish to improve public services often propose giving citizens more choice: of school, of hospital, of pension provider. The reasoning is familiar from markets. Providers who must attract users will try harder to please them, and users who can leave a poor provider will push quality upward simply by leaving. In some services the mechanism works roughly as promised. In others it produces results that surprise its advocates.

The mechanism depends on three conditions that are easy to assume and hard to secure. Users must be able to judge quality, at least roughly; they must be able to act on their judgement at a tolerable cost; and providers must gain something when users arrive and lose something when they depart. Where any condition fails, choice may still be offered, but it will not discipline anyone.

Consider each in turn. Many public services are bought rarely and judged only in retrospect. A parent chooses a school once for each child and learns its quality years later, by which time switching is costly and the evidence is mixed with everything else that happened in the child's life. Where users cannot judge, providers compete on what can be seen — buildings, brochures, published scores — rather than on what matters. Second, the cost of acting may fall unevenly. Families with cars and flexible jobs can travel to a better school; others cannot, so choice may sort users by circumstance rather than lifting standards for all. Third, if funding does not follow users, or if a popular provider cannot expand, the arrival of new users brings congestion rather than reward, and the departure of others brings relief rather than pressure.

Even where all three conditions hold, choice can shift costs in ways its advocates rarely discuss. Providers that compete for users have an incentive to attract the users who are cheapest to serve: the healthy patient, the able pupil, the pension saver with a large and stable balance. Unless funding is adjusted for the needs of each user, competition may improve the service offered to the easy cases while the difficult ones are passed from provider to provider. Regulators can try to prevent such selection, but the rules required to do so are complex, and providers usually understand their own users far better than the regulators who supervise them.

Choice also has a cost for the users themselves, which is the effort of choosing. Comparing schools or pension funds takes time, information and a certain confidence in dealing with institutions, and these are distributed as unevenly as income. A reform that relies on users to discipline providers will be most effective for those best equipped to choose, and the gap between them and everyone else may widen even as average quality improves.

None of this shows that choice is a mistake. It shows that "choice" names not a single policy but a family of arrangements whose effects depend on details that are usually settled after the slogan has been adopted. A reform that announces choice without securing the conditions under which it works is likely to deliver the appearance of competition without its substance — and may leave those least able to choose with providers that others have abandoned.

m3-rc2.title: Passage: Coral spawning and the moon
m3-rc2.html:
Passage: Coral spawning and the moon

On a handful of nights each year, many corals on a reef release their eggs and sperm into the water within the same hour or two. The synchrony is remarkable because corals have no nervous system in the usual sense and no means of seeing one another. Each colony must read the same environmental cues and respond to them in the same way. For decades researchers have tried to work out which cues matter.

Temperature sets the season. As water warms in spring, colonies mature their gametes, so that by early summer they are ready to spawn. But a season is too broad a window: if colonies released their gametes on any warm night, the chance that eggs and sperm from different colonies would meet would be small. The moon appears to narrow the window to a few nights. Experiments in which corals were kept under artificial moonlight showed that shifting the lunar cycle shifted spawning. Finally, the hour is set by the onset of darkness after sunset, which corals detect through light-sensitive proteins in their tissues.

This layered system has an elegance that invites admiration, but it also has a vulnerability. Each cue is reliable only because its relationship to the others has been stable over long periods. Warming oceans may advance the maturation of gametes so that they are ready before the usual lunar window, or are past their best by the time it arrives. Artificial light near coasts may blur the darkness cue. A colony that spawns on the wrong night does not fail completely; it simply releases gametes into water where few others are present, which for a species that depends on cross-fertilisation amounts to the same thing.

The cues are not equally well understood. The role of temperature has been studied for longest, and the role of darkness has been traced to particular light-sensitive proteins, but the means by which a colony registers the phase of the moon remains partly obscure. Moonlight differs from the dark of a cloudy night by a very small quantity of light, and a colony must distinguish the gradual waxing of that light over several nights from the random variation caused by weather and turbidity. Some researchers suspect that the colonies integrate the cue over many nights rather than responding to any single one, which would make the system robust to an overcast evening but slow to adjust if the relationship between the cues were disturbed.

That slowness matters because the cues are no longer changing together. The moon keeps its schedule regardless of what happens on Earth, and sunset arrives at the same time it always has; it is the temperature cue, and with it the ripening of gametes, that is moving.

Some observers have reported that spawning on certain reefs has become less tightly synchronised in recent years, with different colonies of the same species releasing on different nights. The data are patchy and the causes debated. But if the trend is real, it illustrates a general point: a system that coordinates without communication can lose its coordination without anything visibly breaking.

m3-rc3.title: Passage: The craft of forgetting in law
m3-rc3.html:
Passage: The craft of forgetting in law

Legal systems are built to remember. Statutes, judgments and contracts are recorded so that later disputes can be settled by reference to what was decided before. Yet every mature legal system also contains devices for forgetting: limitation periods after which a claim cannot be brought, the expunging of certain criminal records, the discharge of debts in bankruptcy. These devices are sometimes described as concessions to practicality — evidence decays and witnesses die — but that description misses much of their purpose.

Consider the limitation period. If its only rationale were the decay of evidence, one would expect its length to vary with the kind of evidence involved: short where claims rest on memory, long where they rest on documents. Some systems do make such distinctions, but most limitation rules are surprisingly uniform, and many apply even where the evidence is perfectly preserved. The better explanation is that limitation also protects a different interest: the ability of people to organise their lives on the assumption that old matters are settled. A business that has not been sued for a decade invests, hires and borrows as if it will not be. Allowing ancient claims would make that assumption unsafe for everyone, including those who will never face such a claim.

The discharge of debt rests on a similar logic. A debtor who could never escape her obligations would have little reason to earn more, since every gain would pass to her creditors. Forgiving the remainder may cost those creditors little in practice and gives the debtor a reason to return to productive life. Here forgetting is not a reluctant tolerance of imperfect records but a deliberate design for the future.

The device of expungement shows the same purpose from another angle. A criminal record that follows a person indefinitely makes it hard for her to find work or housing, and those difficulties are themselves associated with reoffending. A rule that clears certain records after a period without further offences therefore serves the public as well as the offender: it removes an obstacle to the very behaviour the criminal law hopes to encourage. The rule does not pretend that the offence did not happen. It declares that, for most purposes, the offence should no longer count.

Each of these devices thus involves a judgement about when the value of remembering is outweighed by the value of allowing people to act as if a matter were closed. The judgement varies by society and by period, and it is often contested, but the existence of such devices in almost every legal tradition suggests that law has always treated forgetting as one of its tools rather than as a defect in its memory.

The rise of permanent digital records has made such forgetting harder to achieve. A conviction expunged from the official register may survive indefinitely in a newspaper archive or a search index. The law can still forget; the wider society increasingly cannot. Whether legal forgetting can retain its purpose when its effects are confined to the courtroom is one of the more interesting questions facing legal systems today.

m3-rc4.title: Passage: Why maps of the poor are rare
m3-rc4.html:
Passage: Why maps of the poor are rare

Most countries produce detailed maps of where their wealthiest citizens live. Property registers, tax records and commercial surveys locate expensive housing and valuable land with precision, because someone has an interest in knowing. The places where the poorest people live are often mapped far less carefully, if at all. Informal settlements may appear on official maps as blank spaces or as land designated for some purpose it has never served.

This neglect is not merely a technical gap. A settlement that does not appear on the map is hard to provide with water, drainage or schools, because those services are planned by reference to mapped streets and registered addresses. Residents without an address may struggle to open bank accounts, receive post or prove where they live when applying for help. Invisibility on paper becomes exclusion in practice.

In recent decades, residents of some settlements have begun mapping their own neighbourhoods, counting households, tracing paths and recording which homes lack toilets or water. The results have sometimes persuaded authorities to extend services that had been denied for years. Advocates celebrate these projects as a form of empowerment, and with reason. Yet mapping is not neutral, and becoming visible carries risks as well as benefits. A precise map of an informal settlement is also a precise map for anyone who wishes to clear it. Residents who count themselves may be counted by others for purposes they did not intend.

Self-mapping has a further complication: maps fix what is fluid. An informal settlement changes constantly as families arrive, extend their homes, rent rooms to newcomers or leave. A survey that records the settlement as it stood on a particular day can quickly become an instrument for deciding who belongs and who does not. Households that arrived after the count may find themselves excluded from any services or compensation that follow, and some communities have responded by insisting that their maps be updated regularly or treated as a starting point for negotiation rather than as a final register.

There is also the question of what the map is allowed to show. Residents may wish to record flooding, the absence of toilets or the distance to the nearest clinic, because these are the facts that support their claims. They may be less eager to record the informal businesses, unregistered rentals and improvised electricity connections on which many households depend, and which authorities could treat as grounds for penalties. The content of a community map is thus itself negotiated, and its makers must decide what visibility is worth the risk.

The experience of such projects suggests that the value of being mapped depends less on the map itself than on who controls its use. Where communities retain a say in how their data are shared and acted upon, visibility has tended to bring services. Where data pass straight into the hands of authorities with other priorities, the same information has occasionally hastened eviction. The question is not whether the poor should be on the map, but on whose terms.

m4-rc1.title: Passage: The value of boredom
m4-rc1.html:
Passage: The value of boredom

Boredom has a poor reputation. It is treated as a problem to be solved, by entertainment for the young and by productivity tools for adults, and the devices most of us carry are designed to ensure that we need never experience it. Yet psychologists who study boredom increasingly describe it not as an absence of feeling but as a signal, comparable to hunger or pain, that tells us something about our situation.

What boredom signals, on this account, is a mismatch between the attention we have available and the demands our circumstances make on it. When a task is too easy, too repetitive or too disconnected from anything we value, attention has nowhere useful to go, and the resulting discomfort pushes us to look for something else. Like hunger, the signal is unpleasant precisely so that it will be acted upon. A person who never felt bored would have no reason to leave an unrewarding activity.

If this is right, the habit of silencing boredom the moment it appears has a hidden cost. The signal is answered, but by the nearest available stimulus rather than by a change in what one is doing. A worker who checks her phone whenever a meeting drags has relieved the discomfort without asking whether the meeting, or her role in it, should change. Repeated often enough, such relief may weaken the link between the signal and the reflection it is supposed to prompt.

Psychologists who study boredom have found that people do not experience it uniformly. Some report it rarely even in dull circumstances, while others find it oppressive in situations that their companions consider pleasant enough. The difference does not seem to lie in how much stimulation each person requires so much as in how well each can direct attention: those who struggle to concentrate find it harder to engage with a task that offers little, and so experience its emptiness more acutely. On this view boredom is less a property of situations than a relation between a situation and a mind's capacity to take hold of it.

This helps explain why boredom is unpleasant rather than merely neutral. An empty hour is not in itself painful; what hurts is the sense that one's attention is idling while something else ought to be happening. Boredom thus contains a kind of judgement, however vague, that the present activity is not worth the attention it demands, and its discomfort is the pressure of that judgement towards a change.

Some writers go further and claim that boredom is the mother of creativity: that the mind, left without stimulation, turns inward and produces new ideas. The evidence for this stronger claim is thinner than its popularity suggests. Studies that induce boredom before a creative task have found modest effects at best, and it is unclear whether they reflect boredom itself or merely the relief of being given something to do. The more defensible position is that boredom is useful as information, not as a source of inspiration — and information is valuable only to those who pause long enough to read it.

m4-rc2.title: Passage: Who owns a recipe
m4-rc2.html:
Passage: Who owns a recipe

Recipes occupy an odd place in the law of creative work. A novel, a song or a photograph is protected from copying as soon as it is made, but in most legal systems a list of ingredients and a set of cooking steps are treated as functional instructions, like the directions for assembling a bookcase, and may be copied freely. A chef who invents a celebrated dish can watch competitors reproduce it the following week without any legal remedy.

Economic theory suggests that this should discourage invention. If creators cannot exclude imitators, why would they invest in creating? Yet restaurant cuisine is notably inventive, and new dishes appear constantly. Researchers who have studied professional kitchens find that chefs rely on informal norms in place of law. Copying a dish exactly without acknowledgement is widely regarded as disreputable, and chefs who do it may find that suppliers, critics and colleagues treat them coolly. Sharing techniques with trusted peers is expected, but passing them on to outsiders without permission is frowned upon.

These norms are effective in a small, interconnected community where reputation travels quickly. They work less well across distances, in large chains, or where the copier has no wish to belong to the community whose disapproval would otherwise restrain him. A chain that reproduces a famous chef's dish across hundreds of outlets may never meet the chef's peers and has little to fear from their opinion.

The fashion industry offers an instructive comparison. Clothing designs, like recipes, receive limited protection in many legal systems, and copying is rapid and widespread. Here too the field is inventive, and some scholars have argued that copying actually accelerates the cycle of fashion: once a style is widely imitated it loses its distinction, and those who wish to stand out must move on to something new. Whether the same mechanism operates in cooking is unclear. A dish does not lose its pleasure merely because others serve it, and diners who return to a favourite restaurant often want the same meal rather than a novelty. The analogy shows that the absence of protection need not stifle creation, but it does not show that the reasons are the same in every field.

Chefs themselves are divided. Some regard imitation as a tribute and a sign that their influence is spreading; others, particularly those whose reputation rests on a small number of signature dishes, see it as a threat to their livelihood. The division often tracks the chef's position in the profession: established figures can afford generosity, while newcomers who have staked everything on one idea have the most to lose from its free circulation.

Some observers conclude that the law should be extended to cover recipes. Others argue that the absence of protection is itself a cause of the field's inventiveness: chefs who cannot rest on a single creation must keep producing new ones, and the free circulation of ideas allows each innovation to be built upon quickly. The evidence does not settle the question, but it does show that the relationship between legal protection and creativity is less direct than the simple economic model assumes.

m4-rc3.title: Passage: Counting the uncounted species
m4-rc3.html:
Passage: Counting the uncounted species

Estimates of the number of species on Earth range from a few million to more than a trillion, a spread that would be embarrassing in almost any other science. The disagreement does not arise because biologists are careless. It arises because the great majority of species have never been described, and the methods for estimating what has not been seen depend heavily on assumptions about it.

One method extrapolates from well-studied groups. If, in a thoroughly surveyed region, there are a certain number of insect species for every species of plant, and if this ratio holds elsewhere, the global count of plants can be multiplied to give a global count of insects. The approach is transparent, but its results are only as good as the ratio, and ratios measured in temperate forests may not hold in tropical canopies or deep-sea sediments. Another method looks at the rate at which new species are described over time and projects when the curve will level off. This method assumes that taxonomists' efforts have been spread evenly, when in practice they have concentrated on large, attractive or economically important organisms.

The arrival of genetic sequencing has changed the problem rather than solved it. Sampling soil or seawater for DNA reveals vast numbers of distinct genetic sequences, many belonging to microbes that have never been grown in a laboratory. But deciding how different two sequences must be to count as separate species is partly a matter of convention, and different thresholds can change totals by orders of magnitude. The trillion-species estimates depend largely on such counts of microbial diversity.

The difficulty is not only practical. Even among well-studied animals, biologists disagree about what a species is. One definition counts as a species any group whose members can interbreed with one another but not with outsiders; another counts any population with a distinct evolutionary history, which can be detected in its genes even when it looks identical to its neighbours. The second definition typically yields more species than the first, and the choice between them is guided as much by the purposes of the classifier as by anything in the organisms. Conservation agencies, for instance, have an interest in recognising distinct populations that would otherwise be grouped with abundant relatives and so denied protection.

For organisms that reproduce without sex, as most microbes do, the interbreeding definition does not apply at all, and the genetic threshold is the only practical criterion. Changing that threshold by a small amount can merge thousands of supposed species into one or split one into thousands, which is why the largest estimates are so sensitive to choices that seem, at first sight, merely technical.

What these difficulties show is not that the question is meaningless but that "how many species are there?" is several questions at once. For animals and plants, estimates are converging on figures in the low millions. For microbes, the answer depends on definitions that have been designed for other purposes and may not suit the organisms in question. A single headline number conceals these differences more than it reveals them.

m4-rc4.title: Passage: The architecture of waiting rooms
m4-rc4.html:
Passage: The architecture of waiting rooms

Waiting rooms are among the most widely experienced and least considered spaces in modern life. Clinics, government offices and railway stations all require people to spend time in rooms whose design rarely receives the attention given to the spaces where the main business happens. The assumption seems to be that waiting is dead time, and that a room for dead time needs only seats and perhaps a clock.

Yet a waiting room shapes how people experience the service that follows. Studies in clinics have found that patients who wait in crowded, windowless rooms with no indication of how long they will wait rate their consultations less favourably, even when the consultation itself is identical. Uncertainty seems to matter more than duration: a predictable twenty-minute wait is often reported as less irritating than an unpredictable ten-minute one. Information about queue length, and a sense that the order of service is fair, can do more to improve satisfaction than shortening the wait itself.

Design also communicates status. Rows of fixed seating facing a counter suggest that those waiting are to be processed; movable chairs, natural light and somewhere to put one's belongings suggest that they are guests. People read these signals quickly and adjust their expectations and behaviour accordingly. Staff in offices with hostile waiting areas report more confrontations, though whether the design causes the hostility or merely reflects an institution that already treats visitors poorly is difficult to establish.

Many of the improvements that matter cost little. A screen that shows the number of people ahead in line, or an announcement that the clinic is running thirty minutes late, gives people the means to plan: to make a phone call, fetch a coffee or simply stop watching the door. Seating arranged in small clusters rather than long rows allows families to sit together and strangers to keep their distance. Even the placement of the reception desk matters; a counter behind glass, raised above the level of a seated visitor, tells people something different from a desk at which they can sit down and speak face to face.

Some institutions have gone further and abolished the waiting room altogether, sending visitors a message when their turn approaches so that they can wait wherever they please. Such systems are welcome where they work, but they assume that visitors have phones, can read the messages and have somewhere else to go. For many people who use public services, the waiting room remains the only place available, and its design continues to shape what the visit feels like.

Architects who have worked on such spaces note that the brief they receive rarely mentions waiting at all. Budgets and attention are allocated to the consulting room, the counter or the platform, and the waiting area is whatever space is left over once those have been placed.

Improving waiting rooms is cheap compared with improving the services they precede, which makes it tempting to dismiss such improvements as cosmetic. But a service is experienced as a whole, and an institution that respects people's time before they reach the counter has already begun to deliver part of what they came for.

m5-rc1.title: Passage: The persistence of the QWERTY argument
m5-rc1.html:
Passage: The persistence of the QWERTY argument

For several decades the arrangement of keys on the standard typewriter keyboard served economists as the leading example of a market locking in an inferior technology. The story ran as follows. The layout was designed for mechanical reasons that soon ceased to matter; a rival layout allowed faster typing; but because typists trained on the standard and employers bought machines for trained typists, no one could switch alone, and the worse design survived. The example was vivid and widely taught.

Later historians questioned almost every part of it. The evidence that the rival layout was faster turned out to rest on a few small studies, some conducted by its own inventor, and later comparisons found little difference. Typing speed depends much more on training than on the arrangement of keys. If the rival was not clearly better, then the market had not locked in an inferior product; it had simply kept a perfectly adequate one.

The interesting question is why the original story spread so far on so little evidence. Part of the answer is that it illustrated a theoretical possibility that economists wanted to discuss. Models showing that markets could become stuck with worse standards were elegant and plausible, and a concrete case made them easier to teach. Once the example was in textbooks, it was repeated rather than checked, each citation lending authority to the next.

The revision did not go unchallenged. Defenders of the original account replied that the absence of clear evidence for the rival layout's superiority did not prove that the two were equal; small studies are weak in both directions, and a layout that had never been widely adopted could not be tested on the large population of experienced typists who would reveal its advantages, if it had any. The point has some force, but it cuts against the original story as much as for it. An example offered as a demonstration of market failure needs evidence that the rejected alternative was better, and a demonstration that rests on the impossibility of testing its central claim is not much of a demonstration.

Other candidate examples of lock-in have fared similarly when examined closely. Rival formats in recording, competing gauges on early railways and alternative designs for nuclear reactors have each been offered as cases in which an inferior option prevailed through historical accident. In each, historians have found reasons, sometimes technical and sometimes commercial, why the winner was a reasonable choice at the time, and the evidence that the loser was clearly better has usually been thinner than the story required. None of these findings disproves the theory. They suggest only that clean real-world cases are rarer than the theory's popularity would lead one to expect.

None of this shows that lock-in never happens. Standards do become entrenched, and switching costs are real. What the episode shows is that a good illustration can outrun its evidence, and that the more neatly an example fits a theory, the less likely it is to be examined. The lesson applies well beyond economics. Disciplines tend to keep a small stock of famous cases, and the fame of a case is not a reliable guide to its accuracy.

m5-rc2.title: Passage: Learning from failure in aviation
m5-rc2.html:
Passage: Learning from failure in aviation
