Commercial aviation is often held up as a model of learning from failure. Accidents are investigated by independent bodies whose findings are published, and pilots are encouraged to report their own errors and near misses without fear of punishment. The result, admirers say, is that every crash makes the next one less likely. Hospitals, courts and other institutions are urged to copy the approach.

The admiration is deserved, but the lessons are harder to transfer than they appear. Aviation enjoys several advantages that are rarely mentioned in the exhortations. Its failures are dramatic and public, so there is strong pressure to explain them. Its systems are highly standardised: aircraft of the same type are nearly identical, and procedures are written in detail, so a lesson drawn from one incident applies directly to thousands of flights. And the people whose errors are reported — pilots — are themselves at risk when things go wrong, which aligns their interests with safety.

Many other fields lack these features. A medical error may harm a single patient privately and be noticed, if at all, much later. Patients differ from one another far more than aircraft do, so a lesson from one case may not apply to the next. And the professional who errs is rarely the one who suffers the consequences. Under such conditions, a reporting system modelled on aviation may collect many reports without producing the cumulative improvement it promises.

The contrast is visible within medicine itself. Anaesthesia, which resembles aviation more than most specialties do, with standardised equipment, a sequence of well-defined steps and constant monitoring by instruments, adopted checklists and incident reporting early and saw marked improvements in safety. Areas of medicine where each case presents differently, and where judgement rather than procedure governs much of the work, have found the same tools harder to apply. The difference is not that one group of doctors cares more about safety than another. It is that the conditions under which reporting produces learning are present in one setting and largely absent in the other.

Reporting systems also depend on trust, and trust is easier to promise than to secure. A professional who reports an error must believe that the report will be used to improve the system rather than to assign blame, and that belief is fragile. A single case in which a report is used against the person who filed it can undo years of encouragement, and in fields where litigation is common, the fear of such use may never be overcome. Those who praise aviation's openness sometimes forget how much institutional work went into making it safe to be open.

This does not mean other fields should ignore aviation's example. It means that what they should borrow is less a procedure than a principle: that errors are signs of weaknesses in systems rather than simply failures of individuals. How to act on that principle will depend on features of each field — how visible its failures are, how standardised its work, how aligned the interests of those involved — that no imported procedure can supply.

m5-rc3.title: Passage: Urban noise and birdsong
m5-rc3.html:
Passage: Urban noise and birdsong

Birds that live in cities sing differently from their rural relatives. In several species, urban males sing at higher pitch, louder, or at different times of day, often starting before dawn traffic begins. The most widely accepted explanation is masking: the low-frequency rumble of traffic drowns out lower notes, so birds that shift upward are heard more easily by mates and rivals.

The explanation is plausible, and experiments support part of it. When researchers play recordings of traffic noise near singing birds, some individuals raise their pitch within minutes, which shows that the change can be a flexible response rather than an inherited trait. But other findings complicate the picture. Higher notes do not carry as far as lower ones, so a bird that escapes masking may still be heard over a smaller area. And in some species, females prefer lower songs, which are associated with larger, healthier males. A male that sings higher to be heard may become less attractive to those who hear him.

These trade-offs suggest that urban song is not simply an improvement forced by noise but a compromise, whose terms vary with the density of the population, the structure of the habitat and the preferences of the listeners. Where birds live close together, a short-range signal may be enough; where they are sparse, the loss of range may matter more than the gain in clarity.

Timing offers a different escape from noise. Some urban birds have shifted their singing earlier in the morning, before traffic builds, or later into the evening, and a few have been recorded singing at night near brightly lit roads. Here too the adjustment has costs. Singing in the dark exposes a bird to predators that hunt by sound and may cut into the time it needs to rest and feed, and it may not coincide with the hours when females are most attentive. A shift that solves the problem of masking can thus create problems of its own, just as a shift in pitch does.

There is also the question of whether urban populations are diverging from rural ones in ways that go beyond flexible adjustment. Young birds of many species learn their songs by listening to adults, so a population that sings higher may pass the higher song to the next generation through learning alone, without any change in its genes. Over many generations, a learned difference of this kind could make urban and rural birds less responsive to one another's songs, and some researchers have suggested that this may be a first step towards the separation of populations. The evidence for such divergence is still preliminary, and other researchers caution that birds moving between city and countryside would tend to blur any difference that began to form.

The study of urban song has broader interest because it shows how quickly behaviour can respond to environments transformed by people. It also shows how misleading a single explanation can be. A change that looks like a straightforward adaptation may involve costs that are hidden unless one asks who is listening, from how far away, and with what preferences.

m5-rc4.title: Passage: The meaning of a signature
m5-rc4.html:
Passage: The meaning of a signature

Signatures were once the chief way of binding a person to a document. A name written by hand was hard to forge convincingly, and its presence on a page signalled that the signer had seen and accepted what was written there. Today most agreements are made with a click, a typed name or a box ticked on a screen, and the handwritten signature survives mainly for occasions that people regard as solemn: marriages, property sales, wills.

It is tempting to see this survival as nostalgia, but it serves a purpose. The effort of signing, small as it is, marks a transition from considering to committing. People sign fewer things than they click, and the act draws attention to the fact that something consequential is happening. Legal scholars call this the cautionary function of formalities: requirements that slow people down so that they notice what they are doing.

Digital agreements have largely abandoned this function in pursuit of convenience. A user who accepts the terms of a service may do so dozens of times a week, and the click that binds her is identical to the click that dismisses an advertisement. The law generally treats such clicks as valid consent, but few people believe they represent the considered acceptance that the older form was meant to secure.

The history of formalities suggests that they have always been a compromise between caution and convenience. Wax seals, witnesses and notaries each slowed the making of agreements and each was relaxed when commerce demanded speed. Legal systems responded by distinguishing between transactions: ordinary sales could be made by word of mouth, while gifts of land or promises without payment required writing, witnesses or both. The distinction rested on the observation that people are most likely to act rashly when they give something away or bind their future selves, and that these were the cases in which a moment of ceremony was most valuable.

Digital systems have largely collapsed this distinction. The same interface is used to accept a trivial licence and to consent to the sharing of medical records, and the user is given no signal that one matters more than the other. Some of the difficulty is commercial: firms that profit from frictionless consent have little reason to introduce ceremony. But some of it reflects a genuine uncertainty about which online agreements deserve a pause, since their consequences are often hidden in terms that few users read and fewer understand.

Some designers propose restoring friction to important digital agreements: requiring users to type a phrase, wait a few seconds or confirm twice. Critics reply that friction will soon become habitual and that people will learn to perform it as absent-mindedly as they now click. The disagreement turns on whether the cautionary effect of formalities comes from the effort itself or from its rarity. If rarity is what matters, adding friction to every agreement would defeat the purpose; it would work only if reserved for the agreements that genuinely deserve it.

pr1-rc1.title: Passage: The replication problem and its uses
pr1-rc1.html:
Passage: The replication problem and its uses

When a large collaboration of psychologists attempted to repeat a hundred published experiments, fewer than half produced results resembling the originals. The finding was widely reported as a scandal, and in part it was one. Some of the original studies had relied on small samples, flexible analyses and the selective reporting of outcomes that happened to reach statistical significance. Practices that had seemed harmless individually, such as trying several ways of measuring an effect and reporting the one that worked, combined to fill the literature with results that were unlikely to be true.

Yet a failure to replicate is not, by itself, proof that the original result was false. An experiment is never repeated exactly. The participants differ, the setting differs, and small changes in procedure that seemed irrelevant to the replicating team may turn out to matter. Defenders of some original findings argued that their effects depended on conditions that the replications had not reproduced, and in a few cases later work supported them. In others the appeal to hidden conditions looked more like a refusal to accept bad news, since the conditions were specified only after the replication had failed.

The difficulty is that both kinds of response sound alike. A researcher who says that an effect appears only under certain circumstances may be describing a genuine feature of the phenomenon or protecting a cherished result, and there is no way to tell from the claim alone. What distinguishes the two is whether the circumstances were stated in advance and whether they generate new predictions that can be tested. An effect that is said to depend on the time of day, the mood of participants and the wording of instructions, with each condition named only after a failure, has become too flexible to be refuted, and a claim that cannot be refuted has ceased to tell us much about the world.

The episode has led to reforms. Many journals now encourage researchers to register their hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting data, so that the distinction between predictions and post hoc explanations is visible. Large collaborative studies, run across many laboratories at once, test whether an effect survives the variation that any single laboratory would miss. These reforms do not guarantee truth, but they make it harder for a field to deceive itself, which is perhaps the most that method can achieve.

There is a further lesson, less often drawn. The original findings that failed to replicate were not hidden; they were published in respected journals, cited widely and taught to students. The problem was not that the field lacked a mechanism for correction but that the mechanism worked slowly, because there was little reward for checking what had already been accepted. A science corrects itself only when some of its members are paid, promoted or praised for doing the correcting, and for much of the period in question they were not.

pr1-rc2.title: Passage: The insurer's dilemma in a warming world
pr1-rc2.html:
Passage: The insurer's dilemma in a warming world

Insurance works by pooling risks that are individually unpredictable but collectively stable. No one knows whether a particular house will burn down this year, but an insurer covering a million houses can estimate with some confidence how many will, and set premiums accordingly. The arrangement depends on two conditions: that the past is a reasonable guide to the near future, and that losses in one place are not too closely linked to losses in another. A changing climate threatens both.

The first condition is weakened when the frequency of floods, fires and storms shifts faster than the records used to price them. An insurer relying on fifty years of claims data will underestimate risks that have grown in the last ten, and the error will be largest precisely where change is fastest. Models that project future hazards can correct for this in principle, but they carry uncertainty of their own, and insurers who price according to them may find themselves charging more than competitors who rely on the past. In a competitive market, the firm that is right too early can lose its customers to firms that are wrong.

The second condition is threatened when disasters grow larger. A wildfire that destroys an entire town, or a hurricane that floods a region, produces losses that are correlated rather than independent. Pooling offers less protection against such events, because the many policies in the pool suffer together. Insurers manage correlated risk by buying reinsurance and by holding capital in reserve, but both become more expensive as the scale of possible losses rises, and the cost is passed on to policyholders.

In the most exposed areas, the result has been a familiar sequence. Premiums rise, coverage narrows, and eventually some insurers withdraw. Homeowners who cannot obtain private insurance turn to state-backed schemes, which were usually designed as a last resort for a small number of hard cases and now find themselves covering a growing share of the market. Such schemes often charge less than the risk would justify, because raising prices sharply is politically difficult, and the shortfall is borne by taxpayers or by surcharges on policies elsewhere.

This has a consequence that is easy to overlook. A premium is not merely a cost; it is a signal. A rising premium tells a homeowner, a buyer and a local government that a place has become more dangerous, and it creates an incentive to build differently, to move or to invest in protection. When public schemes suppress that signal, they also blunt the incentive, and development may continue in places where the risk has outgrown it. Keeping insurance affordable is a reasonable aim, but pursued by holding prices down, it can encourage the very exposure that makes insurance unaffordable in the first place.

pr1-rc3.title: Passage: Literary influence and the anxiety of priority
pr1-rc3.html:
Passage: Literary influence and the anxiety of priority

Literary history is often written as a sequence of influences. A poet reads an older poet, absorbs his manner and then transforms it; the younger writer's achievement is measured by the distance travelled from the model. The scheme is useful, but it carries an assumption that deserves examination: that influence flows only forward in time, from the earlier writer to the later.

In one obvious sense this must be true. A writer cannot be shaped by a book that has not yet been written. But the reputation of earlier writers, and the way they are read, is shaped constantly by their successors. A poet who was regarded in his lifetime as a minor follower of fashion may be rediscovered by a later generation that finds in him an anticipation of its own concerns, and thereafter he is read, taught and anthologised as a precursor. The features of his work that the later writers valued are brought forward; those that did not interest them recede. In this sense the later writer creates the earlier one, not by changing his words but by changing what readers notice in them.

The point is not merely that taste changes. It is that the very category of the precursor is retrospective. No writer sets out to be a precursor; the status is conferred by those who come after, and it depends on their achievement. Had the later movement not occurred, or occurred differently, the earlier writer would have remained what his contemporaries thought him. This creates a peculiar dependence in the canon: the standing of a writer may rest less on his own work than on the success of writers he never met.

Critics have reacted to this in different ways. Some regard it as a distortion, to be corrected by reading earlier writers in the context of their own time, with attention to the conventions they worked within and the audiences they addressed. Others accept it as inevitable and even desirable, on the grounds that a literary work lives only in being read, and reading is always done from a present with its own concerns. The first group risks producing scholarship that is accurate but inert, recovering what a work meant without showing why anyone should now care. The second risks making every work a mirror in which the present sees only itself.

A more balanced position would acknowledge that reading backwards is unavoidable but that it can be done well or badly. To read an earlier poet in the light of later ones is to ask what possibilities in his work were developed and which were not; done carefully, this can reveal paths that were abandoned and that might still be taken. Done carelessly, it reduces him to an early draft of his successors. The difference lies in whether the reader remains curious about what the earlier writer was doing on his own terms, even while noticing what others later made of it.

pr1-rc4.title: Passage: Sleep and the cleaning of the brain
pr1-rc4.html:
Passage: Sleep and the cleaning of the brain

Why animals sleep has long been one of biology's more embarrassing open questions. Sleep is costly: a sleeping animal cannot feed, mate or watch for predators, and yet almost every animal studied sleeps in some form, from fruit flies to whales. A behaviour so widespread and so risky must serve some important function, but the candidates proposed over the past century, from conserving energy to consolidating memory, have each explained part of the evidence and left much of it unexplained.

One of the more recent proposals concerns waste. The brain is metabolically active and produces by-products that must be removed, including proteins that, when they accumulate, are associated with degenerative disease. Experiments in mice suggested that the flow of fluid through the brain, which carries such waste away, increases markedly during sleep, as the spaces between brain cells widen. On this view, sleep is in part a period of maintenance, when the brain does work that is difficult to combine with the demands of waking activity.

The proposal attracted wide attention, partly because it offered a simple, physical answer to a question that had resisted simple answers, and partly because it seemed to link poor sleep with conditions that are feared and poorly understood. It also prompted careful scrutiny. Later studies using different methods questioned whether clearance actually increases during sleep, and some found the opposite. The disagreement turns partly on technique: measuring fluid flow in a living brain is difficult, and the anaesthetics used in some experiments may themselves alter the processes being measured.

Even if clearance does increase during sleep, it would not follow that this is why sleep exists. A function can be served by a behaviour without being the reason the behaviour evolved; a process that takes advantage of an existing period of inactivity is different from one that required it. The waste hypothesis would be stronger if it could explain features of sleep that other theories cannot, such as why sleep deprivation is eventually fatal, or why the need for sleep varies between species in the way it does. It would also need to explain why clearance could not simply proceed more slowly during waking hours, as many other forms of bodily maintenance do. The kidneys and liver clean the blood continuously without requiring the animal to lie still for a third of its life, and a theory that makes the brain an exception owes an account of what is special about it.

The history of the question suggests caution about any single answer. Sleep may have originated for one reason and acquired other functions over time, so that it now serves several purposes, none of which alone explains it. If so, the search for the function of sleep may have been misconceived from the start, and the more productive question is what sleep does in a particular species and how those uses fit together.

pr2-rc1.title: Passage: The craft economy of the city
pr2-rc1.html:
Passage: The craft economy of the city

Writers on modern work often describe a choice between two futures. In one, automation and global trade hollow out manual occupations, leaving a divided economy of highly paid professionals and poorly paid service workers. In the other, technology frees people for more creative work. Both pictures share an assumption: that the skilled manual trades are a remnant of an older economy, destined to shrink as machines improve. A visit to almost any large city suggests that the assumption is at least incomplete.

Cities are full of work that resists both mechanisation and offshoring. The plumber, the electrician, the furniture restorer, the tailor who alters suits and the mechanic who repairs bicycles all perform tasks that require judgement applied to particular, irregular objects in particular places. A machine can make a thousand identical chairs; it cannot easily diagnose why a hundred-year-old chair wobbles, or repair it without destroying what makes it worth keeping. Nor can such work be shipped abroad, since the leaking pipe and the wobbling chair are here. The demand for these services has, if anything, grown as cities have become richer, because wealthy households own more things and have less time to maintain them.

What has changed is the status of the work rather than its existence. In many countries the trades were for a generation presented to young people as a fallback for those who could not succeed at school, and training systems were allowed to decline. The result in some places is a shortage of skilled tradespeople alongside a surplus of graduates whose qualifications the market values less than they were promised. Wages in some trades have risen accordingly, and it is no longer unusual for an experienced electrician to earn more than a junior professional in an office.

It would be a mistake to romanticise this. Much manual work is physically demanding and can be hard to sustain over a long career, and the self-employed tradesperson bears risks that the salaried employee does not: irregular income, no paid leave, the need to find customers continuously. The pleasures of craft are real but unevenly distributed, and they are more often described by those who write about the trades than by those who practise them under pressure.

Still, the persistence of the trades suggests that the usual accounts of the future of work are drawn from too narrow a sample. They describe what happens to tasks that can be standardised, and they extrapolate from these to work in general. A great deal of economic activity consists of dealing with things that are old, broken, unique or inconvenient, and such activity is likely to remain stubbornly local and human. A policy that prepares young people only for the work that machines are expected to leave behind in offices may neglect a large body of work that machines were never likely to take.

pr2-rc2.title: Passage: Monsoon forecasting and its users
pr2-rc2.html:
Passage: Monsoon forecasting and its users

Forecasts of the monsoon are among the most consequential predictions issued anywhere. Hundreds of millions of farmers depend on its rains, and decisions about what to sow, when to sow and how much to borrow are made in its shadow. Over the past few decades, forecasters have improved their seasonal predictions considerably, drawing on better observations of ocean temperatures and more powerful models. Yet the benefits of better forecasts have reached farmers unevenly, and the reasons have less to do with meteorology than with how forecasts are expressed and used.

A seasonal forecast is a statement about probabilities over a large region. It may say that rainfall over a zone covering many districts is likely to be near normal, with a stated chance of being above or below. To a farmer deciding whether to plant a crop that needs steady rain in July, such a statement is of limited use. What matters to her is whether rain will fall on her fields in the weeks after sowing, and a forecast of near-normal seasonal totals is compatible with a long dry spell at precisely the wrong moment. The forecast can be accurate by its own standards and useless for her purposes.

The language of probability creates further problems. A forecast that gives a seventy per cent chance of normal rainfall will be wrong, in the sense that the less likely outcome occurs, about three times in ten. Farmers who acted on the forecast and suffered may conclude that forecasts are unreliable, when in fact the forecast performed exactly as a probability should. Communicating uncertainty honestly can thus erode trust, while communicating false certainty builds trust until the first conspicuous failure destroys it.

Some programmes have tried to close the gap by translating forecasts into advice. Rather than reporting probabilities, they tell farmers in a district that, given the outlook, an early-maturing variety is a safer choice, or that it would be prudent to delay sowing until a certain amount of rain has fallen. Advice of this kind can be acted upon, and studies suggest that farmers who receive it make better decisions on average. But advice embeds judgements about what risks a farmer should accept, and a farmer who could afford to gamble on a high-yielding crop might reasonably make a different choice from one who could not survive a failed harvest.

The broader lesson is that information is not useful merely by being accurate. Its value depends on its fit with the decisions of those who receive it: the scale at which they act, the time at which they must commit, and the risks they can bear. A forecasting service judged only by its skill scores may improve steadily while its users remain no better off. Measuring its success by what users do differently, and with what results, is harder but closer to the point.

pr2-rc3.title: Passage: Constitutions and the dead hand
pr2-rc3.html:
Passage: Constitutions and the dead hand

A written constitution binds future generations to choices made by people who are no longer alive. This feature has troubled democratic theorists since constitutions were first written down. If the people are sovereign, why should the living be governed by rules they did not make and can change only with great difficulty? One famous answer was that each generation should rewrite its constitution afresh. The proposal has never been adopted, but the objection behind it has never been fully answered.

Defenders of entrenchment usually make two arguments. The first is that constitutions protect the people from themselves: majorities, in moments of passion or fear, may wish to suppress rights or concentrate power, and rules that are hard to change slow them down. The second is that stable rules allow citizens and governments to plan. A political order in which basic arrangements could be overturned by any passing majority would leave everyone uncertain about what the next election might bring. Investors, minorities and opposition parties alike have reason to value rules that will still be in force after a change of government, and a constitution that offered no such assurance would encourage each faction to seize what it could while it held power.

Both arguments have force, but neither shows that entrenchment is democratic in any simple sense. The first frankly limits majorities; it is defensible, but its defence is that some things matter more than majority rule. The second shows that stability is valuable, but not that it should be secured by the decisions of a particular generation rather than by some other means. A constitution could, in principle, be stable without being difficult to amend, if its rules were widely accepted.

In practice, the tension is managed less by formal amendment than by interpretation. Courts reading an old text apply its general phrases to circumstances its authors could not have imagined, and in doing so they adjust the constitution to the present without changing a word. This makes the document more flexible than its amendment rules suggest, but it shifts the question of democratic legitimacy from the dead authors to the living judges. Critics who object to the dead hand of the founders may find they have exchanged it for the living hand of an unelected court.

The choice is therefore not between a constitution that binds and one that does not, but between different ways of distributing the power to adapt fundamental law. Some systems make amendment relatively easy and expect legislatures to keep the text current; others make it hard and rely on courts; still others hold periodic conventions. Each places the power to change basic rules in different hands, and each carries its own risks: instability, judicial overreach or the capture of conventions by organised minorities. A constitution that does not change at all is not among the realistic options, since circumstances change whether or not the text does.

pr2-rc4.title: Passage: Photography and the evidence of the eye
pr2-rc4.html:
Passage: Photography and the evidence of the eye

When photography was invented, many commentators greeted it as the end of a long human difficulty: the unreliability of testimony. A painter could flatter, a witness could lie or misremember, but the camera, it seemed, simply recorded what was in front of it. Courts, newspapers and scientists adopted photographs as evidence, and the phrase "the camera does not lie" became a commonplace. It was never quite true, and the ways in which it was false are instructive.

The photographer chooses where to stand, when to press the shutter and what to leave outside the frame. A photograph of a crowded square taken from one angle may suggest a mass demonstration; another, taken a few metres away, may show a thin gathering against empty streets. Neither image is false in the sense of depicting something that did not exist, yet each conveys an impression that the other contradicts. The camera records faithfully what falls within its frame, and this faithfulness lends authority to choices made outside it.

Manipulation of the image itself is almost as old as the medium. Early photographers painted out unwanted details, combined negatives to produce scenes that never occurred and posed subjects to create the appearance of spontaneity. Such interventions required skill and time, and their products could often be detected by experts. Some fabrications nonetheless circulated for decades: pictures of spirits hovering behind sitters, of fairies at the bottom of a garden, of officials who had fallen from favour quietly removed from group portraits. That such images were believed says as much about the readiness of viewers to trust the medium as about the skill of those who exploited it. The authority of photography rested less on the impossibility of manipulation than on its cost: it was easier to photograph a scene than to fabricate one convincingly.

Digital tools have changed this balance. Images can now be altered or generated with little effort, and the result may be indistinguishable from a recording to any viewer who lacks the original files. The predictable response has been a call for technical safeguards: signatures embedded in images at the moment of capture, records of every subsequent edit. Such measures can help, but they shift trust from the image to the system that certifies it, and they work only if those systems are themselves trusted and widely used.

The deeper change may be in how images are read. For more than a century, viewers granted photographs a presumption of truth and required reasons to doubt them. That presumption is weakening, and some observers fear a world in which no image can be believed. Yet the older presumption was always too generous, as the history of framing and staging shows. A culture that asks of every image who made it, from where, and for what purpose may be better equipped than one that trusted the camera, even if it has lost the comfort of that trust.

pr3-rc1.title: Passage: Shifting baselines in fisheries
pr3-rc1.html:
Passage: Shifting baselines in fisheries

A fisherman who began work forty years ago will often say that the sea was richer when he was young. His son, who began twenty years later, says the same of his own youth, though the catches he remembers as abundant were already smaller than his father's. Each generation takes as normal the state of the ecosystem it first encountered and measures decline from there. Over several generations the reference point drifts downwards, and a depleted sea comes to look natural to those who have never known anything else.

Ecologists call this the shifting baseline, and it affects scientists as much as fishermen. Systematic records of fish populations in many regions began only after industrial fishing had already reduced them substantially. A stock assessed as healthy because it has returned to its level of the 1970s may be a fraction of what it was a century earlier. Targets for recovery are set by reference to the data available, and the data available begin, inconveniently, at a point when much of the damage had already been done.

Historical sources can sometimes push the baseline back. Market records, tax ledgers, ships' logs and even restaurant menus have been used to estimate catches and the sizes of fish landed in earlier centuries. Such sources are fragmentary and were not collected for scientific purposes, so their numbers must be interpreted with care. A decline in the average size of fish recorded in market sales may reflect changes in taste, regulation or the gear used, rather than changes in the population. Yet when many independent sources point in the same direction, as they often do, the cumulative picture can be persuasive: many seas once held far larger and more numerous fish than any living person has seen.

The implications are not only scientific. Policies that aim to restore fish stocks must choose a target, and the choice of baseline determines how ambitious the target is. A recovery to the levels of a few decades ago may be achievable within a generation; a recovery to pre-industrial levels may be impossible, since the ecosystem may have changed in ways that cannot be reversed. Choosing the more modest target risks accepting a degraded state as success. Choosing the more ambitious one risks setting goals that no policy can meet, which may discredit the effort altogether.

There is no formula for resolving this choice, but the concept of the shifting baseline at least makes it visible. A target that would have been called modest by an earlier generation of fishermen should not be presented as a return to nature. Being explicit about which past one is trying to restore, and why, is a precondition for honest debate about what restoration can mean.

pr3-rc2.title: Passage: Why referees are disliked
pr3-rc2.html:
Passage: Why referees are disliked

Few figures in public life are as reliably unpopular as the sports referee. Players argue with him, spectators abuse him, and commentators analyse his errors in slow motion. Introducing video review was meant to reduce this hostility by correcting the most glaring mistakes. In several sports it has done the opposite: arguments over decisions have multiplied, and the referee's authority, far from being restored, has been further eroded.

Part of the explanation is that video review changes the question being asked. Before it, a referee's decision was final because nothing better was available; spectators might disagree, but they accepted that a judgement had to be made in real time by someone who saw the play once. Once a slower, more detailed view is possible, every decision becomes provisional, and the standard of correctness shifts from what a competent official could see to what a camera can reveal. Many incidents remain ambiguous even on replay, but the existence of the replay implies that a right answer exists, and those who dislike the outcome conclude that it has been missed.

There is also the matter of rules written for the naked eye. Many rules depend on concepts such as intent, control or clear advantage that were designed to be applied quickly by a person watching the play. Examined frame by frame, these concepts become harder rather than easier to apply. A defender's arm that seemed natural at full speed may look deliberate when frozen, and an attacker who was level with the last defender to any human observer may be found offside by a few centimetres on a line drawn by software. The technology provides precision that the rules were never meant to bear, and decisions that are precise in this sense may strike fans as absurd.

Defenders of review reply that the errors it corrects are real and that fairness requires correcting them. This is true, but fairness in sport has always included a tolerance for a certain kind of error, the kind made in good faith by an official in a position no better than the players'. That tolerance helped sustain the authority of the referee, since everyone understood that he was doing a difficult job under the same conditions as everyone else. Review replaces this shared limitation with an asymmetry: the officials in a remote room see what no one on the pitch could, and they are judged by a standard that the players themselves never met.

None of this means that video review should be abandoned. It means that its effects depend on how it is used: on whether it is confined to clear and consequential errors, whether the rules it applies are revised for the precision it offers, and whether those who watch understand that a replay can reduce error without eliminating judgement.

pr3-rc3.title: Passage: The puzzle of cooperation among strangers
pr3-rc3.html:
Passage: The puzzle of cooperation among strangers

Human beings cooperate with unrelated strangers on a scale unknown in other animals. We pay taxes that support people we will never meet, follow rules when no one is watching, and contribute to causes whose benefits we will not share. For evolutionary biologists this is a puzzle, because natural selection is usually expected to favour individuals who take the benefits of cooperation without paying its costs. Explanations for cooperation among relatives, or among individuals who interact repeatedly and can return favours, are well established. Cooperation among strangers who will not meet again is harder to explain.

One family of explanations emphasises reputation. Even if I will never meet a particular stranger again, others may observe how I treat him, and my reputation for fairness may bring me partners and benefits in the future. Experiments show that people behave more generously when they believe they are being watched, and even an image of eyes on a wall can increase contributions to an honesty box. On this view cooperation among strangers is an extension of reciprocity: the return comes not from the person helped but from the wider community that observed the help.

A second family emphasises norms and their enforcement. Human groups develop rules about fair behaviour and punish those who violate them, sometimes at a cost to the punisher. Experiments in which participants can pay to reduce the earnings of those who behave unfairly find that many are willing to do so, even when they gain nothing. If enough people punish violators, cooperation becomes the safer strategy, and the norms become self-sustaining. The puzzle then shifts from cooperation to punishment, since the punisher bears a cost for a benefit shared by all.

A third account appeals to competition between groups. Groups whose members cooperate may outcompete groups whose members do not, and if the differences between groups persist, through culture rather than genes, cooperative practices may spread even if they are costly to individuals within each group. Critics argue that the conditions required for such group-level selection are restrictive and that the evidence for them is disputed. Groups must differ consistently in their practices, those differences must outlast migration and intermarriage, and competition between groups must be intense enough to outweigh the advantage that free riders enjoy within each one.

The three accounts are often presented as rivals, but they need not be. Reputation makes punishment cheaper, since a person known to punish cheats may be cheated less often; norms specify what counts as a good reputation; and competition between groups may favour those whose norms and reputational systems work best. The more interesting question may be not which mechanism explains human cooperation, but how they came to reinforce one another in a species whose capacity for language allowed reputations to travel far beyond the people who witnessed an act.

pr3-rc4.title: Passage: The life of scripts
pr3-rc4.html:
Passage: The life of scripts

A script is often thought of as a neutral tool for recording a language, chosen for its convenience and replaceable by any other that does the job. History suggests otherwise. Scripts carry religious, political and cultural associations, and changes of script have frequently been occasions of intense conflict. A single language may be written in different scripts by communities that wish to mark themselves as distinct, and two closely related languages may be kept apart, in their speakers' minds, largely by the fact that they are written differently.

The connection between script and identity has practical consequences. A government that changes the official script of a language cuts its citizens off, within a generation, from much of what was written before. Older books, documents and inscriptions become legible only to specialists, and the past is mediated by those who choose what to transcribe. Reformers who have made such changes have sometimes intended exactly this effect, presenting a new script as a break with a past they wished to leave behind. Others have pursued efficiency or literacy and discovered the cultural costs only later.

Arguments about efficiency are themselves less straightforward than they appear. An alphabetic script with a small number of letters is often said to be easier to learn than a script with thousands of characters. In a narrow sense this is true, since a learner can begin reading sooner. But a script that represents meaning more directly may allow speakers of mutually unintelligible varieties to read the same texts, and a script that fits the sound structure of one dialect may serve others poorly. What counts as efficient depends on what the script is expected to do and for whom.

Digital technology has added a new layer to these questions. A script that is not supported by the standard encoding systems, or for which fonts and keyboards are scarce, is at a disadvantage in a world where much writing happens on screens. Communities whose scripts were poorly supported in the early decades of computing often adopted another script for digital use, or wrote their language in Latin letters in ways that varied from person to person. Support has since improved for many scripts, but habits formed in the interim have proved durable. A generation that learned to send messages in improvised spellings does not easily return to a script it seldom used on a screen.

These pressures do not all point in the same direction. Technology can marginalise a script, but it can also revive one, by making it cheap to produce printed materials, fonts and learning tools for communities that could never have supported a traditional publishing industry. Whether a script flourishes may depend less on its intrinsic merits than on the institutions willing to sustain it, and on whether its users regard it as worth the effort of keeping.

s1-rc1.title: Passage: The archive and its silences
s1-rc1.html:
Passage: The archive and its silences

Historians are trained to distrust their sources, but the distrust is usually directed at what the sources say. A chronicle may flatter its patron; a court record may reflect the assumptions of the clerk who wrote it down; a memoir may rearrange events to suit its author. These are problems of testimony, and the discipline has developed elaborate methods for dealing with them: comparison with other sources, attention to the circumstances of composition, the reading of documents against the grain of their authors' intentions. Less attention has traditionally been paid to a prior question, which is why a given document exists at all.

Archives are not random samples of the past. They are the residue of decisions taken by institutions about what was worth recording and what was worth keeping, and those decisions followed the interests of the institutions rather than the curiosity of later scholars. A tax authority recorded those who owned taxable property; a church recorded baptisms, marriages and burials among its own members; a colonial administration recorded the activities it wished to regulate. People who owned nothing, belonged to no recognised congregation or lived beyond the reach of administration appear in such records only when they came into conflict with the institutions that kept them, as defendants, debtors or petitioners. The archive therefore does not merely underrepresent certain lives. It represents them, when it represents them at all, at the moments when they were most constrained.

The consequence is subtle. A historian who reads the surviving records of a marginal group carefully and sympathetically may still reproduce the archive's distortion, because the records available to her are disproportionately records of trouble. A community that appears in the documents mainly through court cases will seem more litigious, more disorderly or more desperate than it was, not because the documents are false but because peaceful lives generated no paperwork. No amount of critical reading of individual documents can correct this, since the problem lies in the composition of the collection rather than in the content of any item within it.

Some historians have responded by turning to sources that were not produced for administrative purposes: songs, oral traditions, the archaeology of households, the marginal notes in account books. These sources have their own biases, and they are often harder to date and interpret than official records. Others have tried to reason explicitly about the gaps, estimating what the archive omits from what it includes, in the way an ecologist estimates the size of a population from the animals that happen to be caught. Both responses accept that silence is itself a kind of evidence, but neither can recover what was never written down.

What the debate has changed is less the methods of research than the confidence with which conclusions are stated. A historian who knows that her sources were shaped by the interests of those who kept them is less likely to mistake the absence of evidence for the absence of a phenomenon, and more likely to ask, of any confident generalisation about the past, whose records it rests on and whose it could not have consulted.

s1-rc2.title: Passage: Why cities grow upward unevenly
s1-rc2.html:
Passage: Why cities grow upward unevenly

It is a common complaint that cities do not build enough housing where people most wish to live, and the usual culprit is regulation. Height limits, zoning rules and lengthy approval processes are said to prevent developers from supplying what the market demands, so that prices in desirable neighbourhoods rise far above the cost of construction. There is good evidence for this view. In many cities the price of an apartment exceeds the cost of building it by a margin that is hard to explain except by restrictions on supply, and places that have loosened their rules have usually seen more construction.

Yet the regulatory account explains less than its advocates sometimes suggest, because the economics of height are not linear. A building of four or five storeys can be built with relatively simple methods. Beyond a certain height, construction requires steel or reinforced concrete frames, deeper foundations, lifts, more elaborate fire protection and more space given over to structure and circulation. The cost per square metre rises in steps, and a developer will build taller only where prices are high enough to cover the next step. In neighbourhoods where prices sit just below such a threshold, removing a height limit may produce little new construction, because the additional floors would cost more than they could be sold for.

This has a counter-intuitive consequence. Relaxing restrictions in a city will tend to produce tall buildings in the most expensive districts, where prices already justify the cost, and comparatively little in the moderately priced areas that many reformers hope to see densified. The new supply may slow the rise of prices at the top of the market, and through a chain of moves it may eventually ease pressure elsewhere, but the visible change will be concentrated where housing was already least affordable. Critics who point to luxury towers as evidence that deregulation helps only the rich are mistaken about the long-run effects, but they are describing accurately what deregulation first produces.

The step-like cost of height also helps explain a pattern that puzzles visitors to many cities: a landscape of low buildings punctuated by isolated towers, with little in between. Mid-rise construction, often regarded by planners as the ideal form for a walkable neighbourhood, falls in the range where building is most expensive relative to the value it creates. In some countries, changes to building codes that allow timber frames or single staircases in buildings of moderate height have made such construction cheaper, and mid-rise housing has expanded accordingly.

None of this is an argument for keeping restrictive rules. It is an argument that regulation is one constraint among several, and that a reform which removes it may disappoint those who expected supply to respond evenly. Where the aim is more housing in particular kinds of neighbourhood, attention to the technical and financial thresholds of construction may matter as much as attention to what the rules permit.

s1-rc3.title: Passage: Tact and truthfulness
s1-rc3.html:
Passage: Tact and truthfulness

Moral philosophers have long been divided over whether it is ever permissible to lie. A strict tradition holds that a deliberate falsehood wrongs the person deceived, whatever its motive, because it treats that person's reason as an obstacle to be managed rather than a faculty to be respected. Its critics reply with examples in which the refusal to lie seems monstrous, such as the murderer at the door asking where his intended victim is hiding. The debate is usually conducted at these extremes, with the strict view defended by appeal to principle and attacked by appeal to catastrophe.

Much of ordinary moral life, however, takes place far from such cases, in the territory of tact. A friend asks whether we enjoyed the dinner she cooked; a colleague asks what we thought of a presentation that went badly; a relative shows us a photograph of a newborn who is not, in truth, beautiful. In such cases few people tell a flat lie, and few tell the unvarnished truth. They choose what to emphasise, praise the effort rather than the result, answer a slightly different question from the one that was asked. These manoeuvres are so common that we rarely notice them, yet they are not obviously compatible with the strict view, since they aim, quite deliberately, at leaving the other person with an impression that is kinder than the truth.

Defenders of strictness sometimes argue that tact is permissible precisely because it avoids literal falsehood. The speaker who says "you must have worked so hard on this" has said nothing untrue, and the listener remains free to draw her own conclusions. But this defence makes the morality of an utterance depend on a technicality. If what is wrong with lying is that it manipulates another person's beliefs, then a carefully chosen truth that is designed to produce a false belief manipulates no less than a lie does. Either tact is often wrong, or the strict view has misidentified what makes lying wrong.

There is a third possibility, which is that tact works within a shared understanding. Both parties to a polite exchange usually know its conventions. The cook who asks about her dinner does not expect a restaurant review, and the answer she receives is understood by both as an expression of goodwill rather than a report. On this view tact does not deceive, because the listener is not led to believe anything false about the dinner; she is reminded of something true about the relationship. The view has the merit of explaining why tact feels different from lying. Its weakness is that conventions are not always shared. A person who genuinely wants an honest assessment, and is given a polite one, has been misled, whatever the speaker intended, and the speaker who cannot tell which kind of question is being asked has no rule to fall back on.

The lesson may be that truthfulness is less a matter of individual sentences than of the relationship within which they are spoken. A friend who is always tactful may become someone whose praise means nothing; one who is never tactful may become someone whose honesty is unbearable. The difficult skill lies not in following a rule about falsehood but in knowing what the other person is really asking.

s1-rc4.title: Passage: The slow science of soil carbon
s1-rc4.html:
Passage: The slow science of soil carbon

Soils hold more carbon than the atmosphere and all living plants combined, and small changes in the amount they store could matter a great deal for the climate. This simple fact has made soil carbon an attractive target for policy. Farmers who adopt practices said to increase it, such as reduced tillage, cover crops or the spreading of compost, can in some places sell credits to companies seeking to offset their emissions. The idea is appealing: agriculture, usually counted among the sources of greenhouse gases, could become part of the solution, and farmers would be paid for improving their land.

The difficulty lies in measurement. The carbon content of soil varies enormously from one metre to the next, depending on texture, moisture, past use and the activity of roots and microbes. A change of the size that a new practice might produce in a few years is small compared with this variation, so detecting it requires many samples, taken to a consistent depth, before and after the change. Such sampling is expensive, and many credit schemes rely instead on models that predict the gain from the practice adopted. The models are calibrated on field trials, but the trials were conducted on particular soils in particular climates, and their results do not always transfer.

Depth adds a further complication. Some early studies of reduced tillage found that carbon increased near the surface, where most samples were taken, but later work that sampled more deeply found that much of this gain was offset by losses lower down. Ploughing had mixed carbon through the soil; stopping it concentrated carbon near the top without necessarily increasing the total. A scheme that pays for surface gains may thus pay for a redistribution rather than an addition.

There is also the question of permanence. Carbon stored in soil can be released again if practices change, if the land is sold to a farmer with different methods, or if a warmer climate speeds the decomposition of organic matter. An emission avoided by not burning fuel stays avoided; carbon added to soil remains there only as long as the conditions that put it there persist. Credit schemes address this by requiring commitments over many years or by holding back a share of credits as insurance, but neither device can guarantee what will happen to a field over the century or more during which the offset emission continues to warm the planet.

None of this means that practices which build soil carbon are worthless. Many of them improve fertility, reduce erosion and help soils retain water, benefits that justify them regardless of their effect on the climate. The problem lies in treating the carbon they store as equivalent to a tonne of emissions avoided, so that a company may continue to emit in exchange for gains that are uncertain in size and duration. Soil carbon may be best regarded as a valuable addition to efforts to cut emissions rather than a substitute for them.

s2-rc1.title: Passage: The economics of attention in news
s2-rc1.html:
Passage: The economics of attention in news

For most of the twentieth century, a newspaper sold two products at once. It sold news to readers and it sold readers to advertisers, and the second sale paid for most of the first. The arrangement had a curious consequence: the paper's revenue depended on how many people bought it, but not much on which articles they read. A reader who bought the paper for the sports results subsidised the foreign correspondent whose dispatches she never opened. Editors could therefore publish reporting that few people wanted, on the reasonable assumption that the bundle as a whole would sell.

Digital distribution unbundled the product. Each article now travels separately, through search engines and social feeds, and each can be measured: how many people clicked, how long they stayed, whether they shared it. Advertising, too, is sold against individual pages rather than the publication as a whole. The subsidy that once flowed invisibly from popular sections to unpopular ones has become visible, and an article that attracts few readers is now recognisable as a cost rather than as part of a package.

It would be easy to conclude that measurement has simply made news more trivial, and there is some evidence of this. But the more interesting effect is on what counts as an audience. A local council meeting, reported in print, reached every subscriber who glanced at the page; reported online, it reaches the few hundred people who search for it. Those few hundred may be precisely the people who care most: residents affected by a planning decision, officials whose conduct is under scrutiny. Measured by clicks the report is a failure; measured by its consequences it may be among the most valuable things the publication does. The metrics are not wrong about how many people read the article. They are silent on why it mattered.

Some publications have responded by moving towards subscriptions, on the theory that readers who pay directly will value the reporting that advertising cannot support. The model has succeeded for a small number of national titles with large and affluent audiences. For most local outlets the numbers are harder. A town of fifty thousand people may contain enough readers to support a newspaper through advertising but not enough willing subscribers to sustain a newsroom, especially when much of what the paper reports can be found, in summary, for free elsewhere.

The result is a peculiar pattern of abundance and scarcity. National and international news, which is reported by many outlets and can be monetised at scale, is more plentiful than ever. Reporting on institutions that affect small populations, such as school boards, district courts and municipal budgets, has thinned in many places to almost nothing. This is not a failure of demand in the usual sense. It reflects the loss of a mechanism that once allowed the many to pay, unknowingly, for information whose value lay in its use by the few.

s2-rc2.title: Passage: Domestication as a two-way process
s2-rc2.html:
Passage: Domestication as a two-way process

The domestication of plants and animals is usually told as a story of human mastery. People selected the wild grasses whose seeds stayed on the stalk, the wolves that tolerated their presence, the goats that could be penned, and over many generations they turned these species into crops and livestock suited to human purposes. The story is not false, but it describes only one direction of a relationship in which influence ran both ways.

Consider the cereals. Harvesting a wild grass whose seeds stay attached to the stalk until cut favours plants with that trait, because those are the seeds that end up in the next year's planting. The early farmers who did this were not necessarily aiming at the result; they were simply harvesting what was easiest to gather, and the plants that suited the method multiplied. At the same time, the crops reshaped the people who grew them. Settled cultivation required fixed dwellings, storage, the defence of fields and a calendar organised around sowing and harvest. Skeletal remains from early farming communities often show signs of heavier labour, poorer dental health and shorter stature than those of the foragers who preceded them. If domestication was a bargain, the human side of it was not obviously advantageous in the short term.

This has led some writers to describe domestication as something done to humans as much as by them, and to note with some irony that wheat now covers vast areas of the earth, cared for by a species that devotes enormous effort to its propagation. The image is provocative, but it should not be taken literally. Plants have no intentions, and talk of wheat domesticating people is a metaphor for the fact that a practice, once adopted, created conditions that made it hard to abandon. Growing populations depended on the harvest; land cleared for fields could no longer support the game and wild plants that foragers had used; knowledge of foraging faded within a few generations. The trap, if it was one, was built from the accumulated consequences of reasonable choices.

The two-way view also changes how we think about animals. Dogs, it now seems likely, were not simply captured and tamed. Wolves that were less fearful of people could scavenge around their camps, and over time such populations diverged from their wilder relatives. Humans selected dogs, but dogs also selected humans: the groups that tolerated them gained protection and help in hunting, and these benefits may have shaped which communities flourished.

None of this denies that humans, unlike their crops and animals, could reflect on what they were doing. But reflection came late in a process that had begun without anyone intending it. The history of domestication may be better understood as the gradual formation of a partnership whose terms neither party chose than as the triumph of human design over nature.

s2-rc3.title: Passage: The limits of explanation in music
s2-rc3.html:
Passage: The limits of explanation in music

Musicians have long been wary of explanations of music, and their wariness is often mistaken for anti-intellectualism. It is not. Few performers object to analysis that describes how a piece is built: the key relationships that organise a sonata, the rhythmic patterns that give a dance its character. What they resist is the suggestion that such description accounts for why the music moves us, as though one could understand a joke by diagramming its grammar.

The suspicion has some basis. Analysis is good at identifying features that recur, because recurrence is what makes a feature visible. It is less good at the particular moment in a performance where a phrase is held a fraction longer than expected and a listener's breath catches. That effect depends on the expectation the music has built up, on the performer's timing and on the listener's attention at that instant, and a description of the score cannot capture it, because the score does not contain it. Two performances of the same notes can produce entirely different experiences, and the difference lies largely in features that notation leaves undetermined. A composer can mark a pause or a slowing, but not its exact length, and the same marking is realised differently by every performer who has ever played it.

Yet the resistance can be overstated. Listeners who learn to hear the structure of a piece often report that their experience deepens rather than diminishes. Knowing that a theme will return, transformed, after a long departure allows a listener to feel the return as a homecoming rather than as a repetition. Analysis, in such cases, does not explain the emotion so much as prepare the ground for it. It trains the listener to perceive relationships that the untrained ear passes over, and the perception is itself part of what is felt.

There is also a more modest role for explanation, which is to make articulate what performers already know. Teachers who can say why a passage should be shaped one way rather than another pass on more than those who can only demonstrate, because the student can carry the reasoning to music the teacher never played. Such reasoning is rarely complete; it typically stops at a point where the teacher says that it simply sounds better. But a partial explanation that guides practice is not worthless merely because it does not reach all the way down.

The dispute may thus rest on a confusion about what explanation is for. If it is meant to replace the experience of music with an account that could be understood without listening, it will fail, and musicians are right to resist it. If it is meant to direct attention, refine perception and transmit skill, it has a long and useful history, and the musicians who distrust it most often rely on it, without naming it, every time they teach.

s2-rc4.title: Passage: Trust in numbers
s2-rc4.html:
Passage: Trust in numbers

Modern governments rely heavily on numbers. Unemployment rates, inflation figures, school rankings and hospital waiting times are published, debated and used to allocate resources and judge performance. The reliance is often attributed to a faith in objectivity, as though officials believed that numbers simply describe reality while words distort it. A more interesting explanation is that numbers are used precisely where trust in judgement is weak.

Where officials share a common background, know one another and are trusted by the public, decisions can rest on discretion. A senior civil servant may decide which schools need more funding on the basis of her experience, and her decision will be accepted because she is believed to know what she is doing. Where such trust is absent, because the public suspects favouritism or because decisions must be defended to outsiders, discretion becomes a liability. A rule that allocates funds according to a published formula protects the official from accusations of bias, even if the formula captures less than her judgement would have. The number is less accurate but more defensible.

This explains a pattern that might otherwise seem puzzling: quantification tends to advance not where expertise is strongest but where it is most exposed to challenge. Professions secure in their authority, such as medicine for much of the twentieth century, could resist external measurement; those whose standing was contested, or who answered to a sceptical public, adopted numbers more readily. The move to quantify can thus be read as a sign of weakness rather than strength, a way of borrowing the authority of impersonal method when personal authority is insufficient.

The trade has costs. A formula can only use what can be counted, and the things that are easiest to count are not always the things that matter most. Once a number determines rewards, those subject to it learn to improve the number, sometimes at the expense of what it was meant to indicate. Hospitals judged by waiting times may find ways to start the clock later; schools judged by examination results may teach to the test. The original judgement that the formula replaced would have noticed such manoeuvres; the formula cannot.

Yet it would be wrong to wish simply for a return to discretion. The trust that made discretion workable was often the trust of a narrow group in its own members, and the decisions it produced could be partial in ways that its beneficiaries did not notice. Numbers opened decisions to scrutiny by people who had previously been excluded from them. The task is not to choose between numbers and judgement but to recognise what each can and cannot do, and to resist the temptation, common to both, of treating a defensible decision as if it were a correct one.
